speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. M. J.COLDWELL (Rosetown-Biggar): Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent). It was announced over the radio this morning that Mr. Attlee had made a statement to the effect that there will be a meeting of commonwealth prime ministers this autumn. Has the Canadian government been approached in regard to the matter, and if so, can the minister indicate the purpose of the meeting?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANNOUNCEMENT OF AUTUMN MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should reply to the question. For some little time past the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom has been seeking to arrange a meeting in London of the prime ministers of the British commonwealth during either the summer or the autumn months. My hon. friend will have noticed a statement by Mr. Attlee that he had not found it possible to arrange for the meeting during the summer months on account of inability to get the different prime ministers together at that time, but that he does expect a meeting to be held in October.
I presume the meeting will be similar to the meeting of prime ministers held two years ago, and that it will be one in which matters of general interest to all the nations of the commonwealth will .be discussed. I am not aware, however, that any definite agenda has thus far been arranged.

maintopic: COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANNOUNCEMENT OF AUTUMN MEETING
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Will the Prime Minister himself represent Canada at the October meeting?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANNOUNCEMENT OF AUTUMN MEETING
speechtext: Well, that is something I wish I were in a position to answer. I might say that in the correspondence with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom he was kind enough to express the wish that I might personally attend. I explained the position I was in with respect to attending any meeting in August, because of the convention to be held at that time. As to what it may be thought best to do thereafter may best be decided, I should think, after that meeting. I have expressed my desire to be as accommodating as it is possible for me to be in helping to .bring about the meeting at a time which would be most convenient for the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and the other prime ministers.

maintopic: COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANNOUNCEMENT OF AUTUMN MEETING
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Would the Prime Minister head the Canadian delegation to that conference?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANNOUNCEMENT OF AUTUMN MEETING
speechtext: It will not be a delegation. What is desired is a meeting of the prime ministers. Whoever is in that office at that time will, I assume, represent Canada.

maintopic: COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ANNOUNCEMENT OF AUTUMN MEETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of what has been said about the possibility of the Prime Minister himself attending the conference of prime ministers in the fall in his capacity as prime minister, would it not be just as well to cancel the Liberal convention at Ottawa, which would serve no purpose?

speechtext: Perhaps the minister would give us a few details of the capital cost of $3,000,000 odd in vote 805. speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
Votes 307, 308, 804 and 805 have to do with the international shortwave service of the broadcasting system. Last night I think I explained pretty well what the functions of the international short wave were, and the work that was being done by that organization in broadcasting programs from Canada, to different parts of the world. I explained that the money that was spent prior to 1945, when the international shortwave was opened, was money which had been voted by parliament for the original construction, and arrangements were made that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should operate the service for a reasonable fee percentage of the amount of money spent on the system.
That is as far as that particular development went, inasmuch as no provision was made at that time for offices, either engineering or administrative, or for studios for those who were to take part in broadcasting the programs. It was necessary to use the facilities of the C.BjC. in the city of Montreal, which is the headquarters for the broadcasting, and that was done. Our arrangements in that city have not been of the best, since we have had to have seven different locations in Montreal for C.B.C. and the international short wai*e. Unfortunately last January there

Supply-National Revenue
was a fire and an explosion at one of these locations, in King's Hall on St. Catherine street, involving loss of life and great destruction of property. It immediately became necessary to find other quarters to take the place of those destroyed. AVe have also run into difficulties in that our leases were expiring this year and it became necessary to look for new quarters or to renew the present leases. AVhen it came to renewing leases we found that in Montreal as in many other cities the rates had almost doubled. It was thought that it would be a matter of good policy if the facilities of both the international short wave and the C.B.C. could be brought together in one public building. With that in mind arrangements have been made, but have not been fully completed, under which the crown is buying what is known as the Ford hotel on Dorchester street for headquarters of the international shortwave system. In the building will be housed those offices which are necessary to carry on the system. There will be administrative offices and engineering offices. The interior of the building will be converted into up-to-date studios. The C.B.C. will become tenants of the building. AVhen the C.B.C. become tenants of the building owned by the crown in the name of the international short wave we shall have reached what we have had in mind for years, namely, the idea of having concentrated in one quarter the facilities of both the international short wave and the C.B.C.
As I said, the cost of the building is $2,000,000. In addition to that, to provide for expansion in years to come, if it is necessary, we have also purchased a building from the same people next to the Ford hotel on Dorchester street for the sum of $50,000. In order to take care of the leases which are held by tenants at the present time the Ford hotel people are looking after them and we are compensating them to the extent of $150,000. The cost of the Ford hotel, the cost of the building next to it, and the amount necessary to take care of the leases, bring the total up to $2,200,000. We are asking for an appropriation of $3,000,000 because it will take the remaining $800,000 to reconstruct and transform the building into offices and suitable studios.
I do not know that I can give any more information with reference to the matter, but I shall be glad to answer any questions that have to do with it.

speechtext:
I do not think anybody in Canada begrudges the money to our international short-wave system. It can be one
of the greatest things for good that we have ever had in Canada in connection with trade if it is properly carried on and if the broadcasts are properly done. We are a democratic country. We must let the people of the rest of the world know what a fine place Canada is in which to live. When you listen to some of the members of the C.C.F. party to my left talk about Canada you would think that it was an awful place.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: It is getting better every day.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I find that most people look upon Canada as a good place in which to live. We should be broadcasting to the world what a fine place Canada is.^ I am all in favour of money being expended in that way.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: And a good government to do it.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
You will have a better government when we get into power, which will not be long from now.
Aside from this political stuff, there is one thing we should stop, and that is this farcical method of collecting radio fees. At the present time the broadcasting corporation is purchasing a building for the short-wave system. That is just nonsense because they are going to have the C.B.C. as tenants, and the people of Canada are going to pay for it. They will not get it out of the $2.50 that every radio owner is supposed to pay each year. The system does not get $2.50 from everybody. Let us cut it out. I know that the minister is anxious to cut down expenditures, but how in the world can he justify the expenditure of $571,000 to collect the licence fees? For some unknown reason-I do not know what it is

he says he wants to keep the C.B.C. free of government interference or something like that. The point is, it is not done. A person can have ten radios, and he pays a fee of $2.50. If he gets one more radio in his car he has to pay an additional $2.50.
The Minister of Agriculture probably has three or four radios in his house and one in the hotel. I have two or three around my place as well; I have one in my summer home and on my farm. All I have to pay is $2.50. What a nonsensical situation that is. I cannot understand it. I am all in favour of having a good C.B.C. AVe should have had a radio committee this year. It should be a standing committee. That committee should meet every session because there are many things that are dependent upon the C.B.C. There is the question of freedom of speech, which is coming up all the time. AVe have that question before us now.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
Radio has been an interesting subject to me throughout the past number of years. I rise to make only one observation, and perhaps ask a question. No radio committee was set up this year, in spite of the fact that last year and every year that the radio committee has met it has recommended that the radio committee of parliament be an annual affair. Because that committee was not set up, we have not had an opportunity to go into the receipts and expenditures of the C.B.C. and the general radio policy as it exists in Canada from time to time.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a tremendous institution. While it is in the commercial field, and is reaping revenues by being in that field, it has not yet been able to stand on its own feet. I am not making any harsh criticism, because I recognize that the corporation is doing a job which requires expenditures over and above what a properly operated radio system might require. Nevertheless, with the operation of the short wave station included, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is becoming a tremendous drain upon the taxpayer. I believe that somewhere along the line we have to call a halt.
I am all in favour of making Canada known to the other nations of the world. I am all for the use of the short-wave system to encourage proper trade relations between Canada and the rest of the world. I am all for letting the rest of the world know something about our Canadian culture. Many of us wish it were of a higher order, but perhaps, in a small nation of 12,000,000 people, we cannot expect too much in too short a time. I am all for these things.
When however we begin to look into the amount of money spent on the Canadian

Broadcasting Corporation I am beginning to think that it is not entirely justified. The C.B.C. and the short-wave station, with its operations, are tied in one with the other. Personally I have not been able to satisfy myself, in reading any of the reports, as to where one ends and the other may begin. There is a general feeling abroad that the short-wave radio station, with its operations, being paid for purely by the taxpayers of Canada, since I understand the short-wave station has no commercial revenues-the minister can correct me on that point-everything the short-wave station does is done at the expense of the people of Canada. Some people who are interested in radio policy in Canada are coming to feel that the shortwave station with its operations is becoming a sort of cow which is fed by the taxpayer but perhaps in the end milked by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
If I am not right on that I would like to be put right, but it will take more than simply an answer of a minute or so to put me right on it, because I do not believe we can get the picture until we are able to go into the entire financial policy, with receipts and expenditures and all that is involved between the C.B.C. on the one hand and the international short wave on the other.
I do not rise to oppose this expenditure, but we have a tremendous capital outlay here, most of which I fancy is for the purchase of the Ford hotel in Montreal. I want to say a word on that-and it is not by way of criticism, because I really do not feel that I am competent to criticize on that particular point. However, I will take it for granted that those who are managing this thing are doing right. I must say that I never did visualize the government taking over the Ford hotel in Montreal. I know that the C.B.C. some years ago had an option to buy a piece of property which at the time they took out the option appeared to be an idle spot. After that there was a readjustment of population, and so on, in Montreal, and they let the option go by the board. This meant that some other arrangement had to be made, but I never expected that- what was going to happen would be the purchase of an old hotel. I visualized, and I recommended years ago, that Canada should have somewhere for its radio operations a sort of young radio city. I rather visualized something unique in architecture, situated perhaps in the middle of an elaborate park or other area of the kind in which art in different forms could be

Supply-National Revenue
exemplified-because after all, radio is to a large extent an art. Instead of that we are getting drab office buildings situated in the midst of a lot of other buildings. Personally I do not like the idea. However, there is nothing I can do about it except to express my thoughts on the subject.
I am surprised at the. location of this building, which now I suppose will have to do the corporation for years to come. I do not like that. Pretty soon the building, situated where it is, will be obsolete, or, if not obsolete, not much of an advertisement for radio in Canada. I rather expected that this young radio city which I visualized in a growing nation would be situated in Toronto. Why it was decided to buy the Ford hotel in Montreal I do not know.

I would ask the minister to say whether I am right in saying that the Ford hotel, while being bought for the short-wave station, is simply a sort of cover. I would not oppose that, because I am not one to oppose the spending of money. I think that is what money is for, to be spent. On the
other hand, when it is to be taken out of the pockets of the taxpayers, they want to know that they are to get something in return. I believe that this is just a suitable way of asking the people of Canada for two or three million dollars, on the basis of a short-wave service, so that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation may come in on the kill. speechtext:
Very well; I shall continue. What I started to say was this. While the amount may appear to be large, and it is a large amount, I believe the expenditure on the international broadcasting station is warranted. Those of us who have followed the activities of this station know that it is giving to the people of the world an idea of Canadian life and culture; but I feel that it has rendered a more valuable service even than that during the last couple of years.
Our international radio station is one which is heard over a larger part of Europe than any other station in North America. For instance, I know from evidence that was given before the radio committee last year that in Czechoslovakia we have the largest group of listeners of any radio station that penetrates into eastern Europe. At this time, without indulging in propaganda of the type to which we are sometimes subjected, the fact that we are able to penetrate into countries behind what is sometimes called the iron curtain is all to the good. In doing that I think the station is rendering a useful service, not only to Canada but to the democratic cause throughout the world. To the extent that we are able to do that we are keeping in touch with people behind the iron curtain who are our friends and who feel that they are plowing somewhat

of a lonely furrow. Consequently anything we can do, through our culture programs and so on, in eastern Europe, indeed all of Europe, will be a valuable service to democracy the world over.
I am glad that several years ago, after a great deal of discussion in the radio committee, the government built the station and the corporation assumed the responsibility for its programs. I am quite sure that if we had a radio committee this year and the members of the corporation appeared before it, they would be able to tell us again the reaction throughout Europe and the rest of the world where the station is heard, and could give us an impressive list of persons who had been engaged and who, because they are refugees to a large extent, must be remunerated. It is one way of doing what I think we should try to do: we should endeavour to assist people in our country who have suffered for the common cause by enabling them to perform a useful function to Canada and to their native land. For that reason alone, if for no other, we should support the international broadcasting station.
Someone suggests that we might get some commercial revenue. I do not think that is possible with an international station. For one thing, in many countries a good example was set in not permitting commercial advertising over the radio. Those countries would resent it if a North American station advertised for sponsors in their countries. I regret exceedingly that the broadcasting corporation this year has changed its policy in that respect, by allowing prices to be mentioned under certain circumstances. I think that is a backward step; had there been a radio committee this year we should have reported adversely upon it. It is unfair to the small merchants, because it places them more and more in the hands of the big companies which can buy advertising in considerable quantities.
So far as short wave is concerned, from what I know and what I have learned from persons who have spoken to their own countries after certain things have happened there, I am convinced that this radio station is rendering a valuable service and that we should support it-if we are anxious, as I am sure hon. members are, to do all we can to encourage and to support the friends of democracy who today are under dictatorships in various parts of the world.

house only in recent days. The question of the purchase of the Ford hotel in Montreal was scouted in this chamber only about two weeks ago. I asked a question about it, based upon some information which had appeared in the press, and I was told that the information was not correct. Further information has appeared subsequently in driblets, and it is only now, within the last several days, that we have had a statement as to the details of the purchase.
A matter of this magnitude, involving the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and of the government with respect to short-wave broadcasting, warranted the setting up of the radio committee. Certainly many of the members who had been on radio committees in previous sessions, were pressed with a multitude of other duties, and were not aware of any extensive change in policy on the part of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Under these circumstances it perhaps did not seem necessary that the committee be convened to meet again this year. Had we been told at an earlier stage of the session that expenditures of this magnitude were contemplated, that changes in policy were involved, or that an expensive building in Montreal was to be purchased, certainly it would have been the duty of the house to press the government to set up the radio committee.
I am not commenting in detail upon the terms of the purchase. Without more information I would not feel competent to express an opinion, although I am inclined to share many of the views expressed this morning by the hon. member for Macleod. But I do say that a transaction of this magnitude should not be permitted without having first a review by the radio committee.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

speechtext: I do not seek necessarily to bring into disrepute the policy embarked upon. Those of us who have regretted, and still regret, the building up of this great monopoly, view with increasing uneasiness the way in which it goes on acquiring more and more properties. This further aspect of it is in one's mind-and for the life of me, I cannot understand what the press is thinking about, because as soon as we get radio newspapers, and they become effective, this great and centralized system of propaganda will have been established.
Let me say quickly that I believe the C.B.C. try to be fair. I am sure they believe they are being as independent as can be. I have no doubt they often think they are leaning over backwards to be fair. But in my opinion it just is not humanly possible for any government controlled corporation to be absolutely independent of government. It just does not happen that way.

I submit that from a business point of view this is an excellent purchase. What the hon. member for Macleod has in mind would, I have no doubt, be pretentious and artistic, and would involve an expenditure of two or three million dollars. maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Is it the intention of the minister to reply to the inquiry I made about the amalgamation or merging of C.B.C. with the national film board?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I do not think the government has given consideration to amalgamating the C.B.C. with the national film board. They are two entirely different set-ups. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is the property of those who pay licence fees for receiving sets and of commercial firms who pay licences. That includes about 95 per cent of the people of Canada, because our coverage is between 95 and 97 per cent of the homes of Canada. That is in an entirely different position from the film board, which is maintained out of the taxes of all the people of 'Canada. It was an agency set up to create and distribute films. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, according to the broadcasting act of 1936, is an entirely separate corporation responsible not to the government but to parliament. They operate wholly-owned and wholly-controlled public systems of broadcasting. The national film board was set up under the National Film Board Act, and it is there to do sponsored work for different departments of government and such other work as the board, which is representative of all parts of the country and of all the services within the government, may be directed to do.

'Mr. MacNICOL: There is nothing in the estimates of the public works department pertaining to great lakes levels, particularly lakes Ontario, Erie and Huron. Since the high water levels of these three lakes, and particularly lake Ontario at the moment, are a matter of major importance, I felt I should raise the question at this time.
Across the front of the great city of Toronto lies what was in my day, when I used to visit it, as I did many hundreds of times, a most beautiful island. No finer public park existed in Canada than Toronto island as it was some years ago. When one recalls seeing over there thousands upon thousands of mothers, scores of thousands of children, all gathered there for the good of their health; when one remembers the thousands of picnics that were held on the island by residents of Toronto many years ago, one wonders why it is that today the island is in such a deplorable condition.
I was over there a few days ago to check up on my past observations, and I am exceedingly sorry to say that the high water level of lake Ontario is now ruining that beautiful island, so that unless some major reclamation program is initiated it will be washed away. At the moment the latest report for the month of June indicates that the water level of lake Ontario, that is to say, Toronto harbour, is at the almost unprecedented height of 248-15

feet above sea level, the highest level in the history of the lake since 1860, except in July 1947 when it averaged 248-81.
What can. be done I am not going to say. I may offer suggestions, but I am quite aware that the problem is a great one. On the island itself, comprising about 800 acres, there were many years ago beautiful lagoons on which the residents of Toronto used to pass their time in pleasure boats, and in my time many thousands of people spent the summer in cottages on the island. Unless some change takes place in the Ontario lake level, all that will be a thing of the past, and it will be a serious matter for the great city of Toronto.
Not only does this apply to Toronto island; the same is true all along the three lakes. Look at Burlington beach, where many hundreds of houses were built; today they are more or less imder water. One sees the same thing all along lake Erie up around Erieau, where I went recently to see the effect of the high water level. But the damage is not confined to the Canadian side; one can see the same thing on the United States side. I am afraid there will be a great deal of trouble.
In 1941, if I remember rightly, I brought up the question of lake levels in the House of Commons, and I predicted then what would happen as one of the results of the diversion of a very large volume of water from the Albany river watershed into the St. Lawrence river watershed. I predicted then that not only this government but the government of the United States would face thousands of legal actions for the destruction of private property, and that is what is coming to pass.
On March 10 of this year an organization known as the Lake Shore Erosion Association held a conference in Toronto. So far as I can estimate from the report, which I have in my hand, between sixty and seventy-five municipalities along the shores of lake Ontario, lake Erie and lake Huron, attended to lay before the conference the troubles which each was having from the constantly rising lake levels. Many resolutions were passed, one of which I will read, No. 7:
Resolved that this organization ask the provincial and federal governments to instruct their engineers to make a survey of erosion on the great lakes and report with a recommendation for remedy; and that in this report be included a report on the effects of the Ogoki and Albany river diversions on the level of the great lakes.
It was about the probable effect of the diversion of waters from the Albany river watershed into the St. Lawrence river watershed that I spoke in 1941 when I predicted that precisely what is happening now would take place. The delegates who framed this resolution probably had before them a pamphlet

Supply-Public Works
I wrote in 1939; for I sent copies of it to many of the municipalities along the great lakes who have written to me on the subject. The pamphlet is called "Water". I gave a copy of it to the minister this morning and I shall be glad to give copies to other members. This pamphlet is a treatise on lake levels. I have travelled over these lakes from one end to the other, as well as to their sources and to the sources of the rivers that flow into them; I know therefore what I speak about. In the pamphlet I discuss the lake levels and the flow of water into these lakes.
This report mentions the Ogoki and Albany rivers. The Albany river watershed is in northern Ontario, flowing from west to east. It is a big river, between 500 and 600 miles long. In some places it is a mile wide. Its principal tributary is the Ogoki river which is about 500 miles in length. I have been on that river from one end to the other. The Ogoki river has an average flow of 4,000 cubic feet per second throughout the year, which means that in the spring the flow goes up to anywhere from 10,000 to 20,000 cubic feet per second, while in the summer it goes down to perhaps 1,000.
Some years ago I took a trip to Chicago, and engineers of the United States government whom I visited said some things that surprised me. At that time I was fighting against the diversion of water from lake Michigan out of the St. Lawrence river watershed into the Mississippi river watershed. Chicago wanted more and more water. At that time they were taking about 12,000 cubic feet per second out of the St. Lawrence river watershed and pouring it into the Mississippi river watershed.
I had gone there to discuss the problem with them and they told me that we would not have to worry very long because they would get all the water they wanted from northern Ontario. That was something utterly new to me and I asked, quite innocently, where they would get it from in northern Ontario. They replied that they expected to divert the waters of the Ogoki river. I hurried back to Toronto and later arranged a trip to the Ogoki river with Mr. Roy Snider of the Toronto Telegram, a wizard in this line of business. We found the place on the Ogoki where the dam was to be located.
Later the question came up in the House of Commons of the Ontario government's proposal to pour more water down the Nipigon river, and I fought that like a tiger. I fought as hard as I could, and for a considerable time I was instrumental, I believe, in preventing the passage of that proposal through this house. Finally, however, this government allowed the Ontario government to do what
I argued was an act against the laws of God, in the diversion of water from one large watershed into another watershed; because in my opinion the waters of the Albany river should not find their way into the St. Lawrence river watershed. But the government finally did agree to the diversion of water from the Albany river watershed into the great lakes, the argument being that it would allow them to develop much more power. I often think of the engineers with whom I was associated at the time we were fighting the diversion of water at Chicago, and of their strong argument that the diversion of that water lowered the levels of lakes Ontario, Erie, Huron and Michigan. I agree with them; they were absolutely right. It amuses me now to hear what some of these same engineers say today. In fact it passes my comprehension how they can say that the pouring of water into the great lakes watershed does not raise the lake levels.
What has happened? At that time, and for quite a length of time before, those who were fighting the Chicago diversion put up a strong battle. They had associated with them all the states along the United States border, including Wisconsin, whose engineers were most vigorous fighters and whom I visited on several occasions at their capital, Madison. Their arguments were strong that the diversion of water at Chicago, which at that time was at the rate of 12,000 cubic feet per second, seriously lowered the levels of the great lakes, and they were right.
Some hon. members will recall the story of that battle, and how it resulted in the United States government agreeing, in order to appease Chicago, to build under the city of Chicago a tunnel perhaps twenty-five miles in length and twenty-four feet in diameter, from the sewage disposal works in the north part of Chicago. The result was that the effluent of the sewage disposal works would pour into the Des Plaines river and go on into the Illinois and down into the Mississippi. That tunnel cost perhaps S150 million. The United States did that so that Chicago would permit them to agree with Canada not to take so much water out of the great lakes watershed; and the United States supreme court issued an order that Chicago should reduce its takings to 1,500 cubic feet per second for dilution purposes. But the city itself was allowed to take for domestic purposes from lake Michigan an additional 2,000 cubic feet per second, or rather the city is now allowed to take a total for dilution and domestic purposes of 3,500 cubic feet per second instead of what they had been taking, 12.000 cubic nw second.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
From the Canadian side, from the immediate watershed of the Nipigon river, which includes Nipigon lake and a string of lakes up north over the height of land, and from the Keno-gami watershed, the Iienogami being a tributary of the Ogoki, we are now pouring into the great lakes watershed 5,200 cubic feet per second, 1,200 cubic feet per second from the Kenogami and 4,000 cubic feet from the Ogoki. Chicago, as I said a moment ago, is allowed to take out at the moment at the rate of 3,500 cubic feet per second, which makes a net increase in the water flowing into the great lakes watershed of 1,700 cubic feet per second. Some hon. members will say that does not amount to a great deal of water, but I say it does. It amounts to a vast volume of water when you realize that it goes on every second of every minute of every hour for 365 days in the year. Actually it amounts to 164 billion cubic feet of water per year. I will not listen to any engineer who says that the flowing into the great lakes watershed of even an additional 50 billion cubic feet of water per year does not mean anything. It does. All these municipalities along the great lakes are alive to that fact.
I read a moment ago resolution No. 7, in which the reference to the Albany and the Ogoki impelled me to show that from these two rivers we are pouring into the great lakes watershed an additional 1,700 cubic feet per second.
Resolution No. 8 reads as follows:
"Whereas it is the opinion of this association that the removal of sand from the beds of the great lakes system contributes to and aggravates the erosion taking place on the shores of the said great lakes and whereas the control of the beds of the lakes is within the province of Ontario.
Mention is made of the question of sand removal, because everyone knows that at east Toronto we have those magnificent Scarboro Bluffs which are being ruined by erosion. West of Toronto all the way to Hamilton, including such places as Port Credit, Long Branch and all along the northern shore of lake Ontario, the shores are being ruined by erosion. The problem of sand is mentioned there because the city of Toronto at the moment is considering (his gigantic problem in connection with the destruction of its own beautiful island. The last day I was there I had to walk on planks where we used to have all sorts of ball games and all sorts of parties. Sand is mentioned because the city of Toronto has under consideration-I do not know who is fathering it-the raising of the level of Toronto island by two feet. It is a big problem. Toronto

island consists of 800 acres. To raise that 800 acres by two feet would require about 80 million cubic feet of sand.
This association is fearful of the pumping of the sand from the lake into the area to build up Toronto island. I shall not make any comment on whether that would mean trouble or not, but I mention it because the Department of Public Works has control over all that area, and it is a problem. Certainly the island must be raised two feet to make it serviceable at all, or else some other major action must be taken.
I want to give some idea of the effect of this diversion. I do not say for one moment that the diversion is the whole cause. Someone will tell of other causes. But to me it is one of the major causes, because I have been at it a long time; I know that the pouring into the great lakes watershed of a net of 1,700 cubic feet per second is bound to have an effect. It may not happen all at once. It took a. long -time coming up, and it will be just as long going down. I believe that the present water level of lake Ontario is not going down very rapidly. As a matter of fact, with the exception of July 1947, it is higher this year than it has been in any previous year since 1860, when the records were first kept. For instance, according to the topographical report I have in my hand, in May 1948 the height of water was 0-37 feet higher than it was in April 1948. It was 0-45 feet higher than May 1947. That is about half a foot higher. It was 0-79 feet lower than the highest May-that of 1870-since 1860. In July 1947 it reached 248-83, and today it is 248-15. It was 4-27 feet higher than the lowest May since 1860, -which was in 1935. In other words, the water level of lake Ontario today is five feet higher than the lowest record. That is a gigantic volume of water. I am particularly interested in the preservation of the beautiful island at Toronto, in my judgment one of the finest parks in the world. But today it is being ruined by these high water levels.
These figures are obtainable from the hydrographic service, and they must be correct or they would not send them out. In May of this year in lake Ontario it was 1-54 feet higher than the average stage of May for the last eighty-eight years. That is a pretty high record. It is stated that the cost of raising the island two feet would be $3,000,000. AVho will pay for it? Certainly the city of Toronto should not have to pay for it. Why should Toronto have to pay for it? The city is not responsible for the pouring of water into the St. Lawrence watershed from the Albany river watershed.

Supply-Public Works
Let me repeat that for years I fought against the Chicago drainage canal diversion being allowed to take out as much water as it did, and these engineers were fighting the Chicago diversion when I argued that taking that water out lowered the lake level. If those engineers were right then, certainly they are wrong today if they say that the pouring of 5,200 cubic feet per second into the great lakes watershed does not affect the water levels of the great lakes. I know that the level of lake Superior is controlled, and I am not speaking about lake Superior. But in respect of the three lower lakes, I maintain that there is no other argument than that the pouring in of that big volume of water has had a bad effect. The fact that Chicago does take out 3,500 cubic feet per second means a net increase in the water of the lower great lakes of 1,700 cubic feet per second.
The fact that these levels are so high is clear evidence that they are affected. Other engineers say that the general tendency will be up. What is to be done about it? What can the department do? I do not know; but I would ask the minister between now and the next session to look into the question, through his engineers. Someone will say it is only half an inch or an inch. But it is always going up. It cannot be allowed to continue. What is the use of Toronto paying moneys out this year to raise the level of the island in front of the city

and no doubt the city will expect the federal government to pay for it-if in another ten years, owing to the continual ingress of water from the Albany river watershed into the great lakes watershed, you have to add another two feet to the top of it?
It is a big problem. I appreciate the minister's allowing me to bring it up at this time; I do not wish to continue any longer, because I want him to finish his estimates. I would however ask him to consider carefully what I have placed on the record, and I would ask that he be not led astray. Let no one tell the minister that the pouring in of that amount of water does not have any effect upon these levels. It has. All he has to do is to check back to the reports submitted by the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario, by the city engineering department in Toronto, and by other engineering bodies, at the time of the fight against the Chicago drainage canal, and he will see that the engineers argued that the taking out of the water at Chicago did lower the lake levels. I shall be amused if they try now to say that the pouring in of additional water does not affect the lake levels. The report showed that the levels are higher today than they have been in the past eighty-eight years.

If I followed well the hon. member's argument, he has said that the diversion of the natural flow of water into the great lakes has brought the levels of those lakes up to an extent that damage is caused to the shoreline and to the island at Toronto. Having explained this to the officials of my department, I received the following answer this morning:
It has been claimed that the high water on lake Ontario is caused partially through a diversion of water from the Little Long Lac watershed and the Lake Nipigon watershed. It is true that water is diverted on to the great lakes system from these two watersheds in the amount of approximately 5,2'00 cubic feet per second; i.e., 1,200 cubic feet per second in the case of the former and 4.000 cubic feet in the case of the latter. This diversion has been going on for approximately four years and it was legalized through an exchange of notes between Canada and the United States, wherein it is admitted that the use of this water for power is solely the property of the Canadian government and is not to 'be divided equally as is the case with the rest of the water in the great lakes-.
In 1941 when -these notes were exchanged it was computed that the diversion would never raise lake Ontario more than three inches, and in order to arrive at this point it would take approximately twelve years. In order to arrive at this figure it must be noted that the small diversion, which is only three per cent of the total flow, will have to assert its influence on each of the lakes in advance of lake Ontario, and it must also be noted that once it has arrived at this predetermined figure of three inches the flow through the St. Lawrence will have been increased to a point that this extra water will not raise the level of the lake any further.
These figures have been checked by the dominion, the province and the United States authorities and, while there are some discrepancies, they all arrive at the same point of a variation of an -inch only.
They were checked this morning as to accuracy with the Ontario hydro.
The water level for lake Ontario during 1947 was extremely high, the July average being 248-8. which is the highest it has been since records have been kept. The average for June this year, to date, is nine inches lower than that of last year.
I am told that this increase in the water level would depend more upon natural causes than the diversion of water. Not being an expert I have to give this answer to the hon. member. I do not ask him to agree with

Mr. Chairman, I presume you do not want me to speak on floods on this item, so I shall confine myself to river bank erosion, hoping to have the opportunity to discuss floods some time this afternoon.
I was much interested in what previous speakers have said, and I join with them in impressing on the government that while under the act set up forty years ago the federal authorities may have no responsibility for river bank erosion, conditions have entirely changed since that time and must be met accordingly. I am not blaming the government for administering the act as is, but I say it is up to parliament to amend the act. I am confining my remarks to conditions in my own riding, but I am sure that many other ridings are similarly situated.
Year after year since 1912, although I did not actively participate at that time, we had been petitioning the federal government and the government of British Columbia about river bank erosion. If I remember correctly, although I had nothing to do with it then, the first action taken in connection with river bank erosion on the Fraser river was in 1912 or 1913. Every year since then, ever since I have been active in political life or have been a member I have been urging the government
Supply-Public Works

to accept responsibility in this matter. I have lost many acres of my own land, on which I paid good taxes, through its floating away down the Fraser river. In the last few years I have seen acre after acre and buildings on the bank of the Fraser river, particularly in Chilliwack and in Kent, float away. The only reply I can get from the department is that the federal government is responsible only for channel clearance and navigation. As I stated the other day, years ago, when the Fraser river was navigable as far as Hope, and before that as far as Yale-that was before my time -we did not have these great sandbars which caused river bank erosion, which is not taken care of by federal government engineers and certainly not by the provincial government engineers.
I should like every member of the house to see pictures taken in 1939. I am not speaking of the floods this year; I shall have plenty to say about them this afternoon. I am talking now about river bank erosion, which has cut right into the dike near the main bridge. I have pictures of the piling put up by the C.P.R. in 1894 and 1896 when they realized that the end of their bridge would go out. I would like members to see a picture taken in 1939 of one span of the C.P.R. bridge.
Another cut was made half way in the farmers' dike through erosion caused by the action of the C.P.R., in spite of the protests of the reeve of the municipality and my representations to the federal Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works. The Department of Public Works replied, up until November of last year, that they had no control over the matter, but in November last they admitted that they had responsibility for the Fraser river causing erosion. I would like to show the minister a picture of the span that went out this year, taking with it one hundred feet of the dike, through the erosion caused by the action of the C.P.R. over a number of years.
I was not in the house on June 9-and a lot of damage was done after that by erosion- but according to Hansard the Minister of Transport said that the railways estimated that already a million dollars' worth of damage had been done to their lines, not to the farms. I do not want to be critical; I do not want to indulge in recriminations, but I believe it is up to parliament, not government, to realize that a lot of changes have taken place since the act was passed. Among other things, the watershed in British Columbia has changed. I do not know so much about other parts of Canada, but I do know that in British Columbia the watershed has changed. When the watershed changes, even the greatest engineers

will admit that the flow of water, through navigable waters or through any other system, adversely affects river bank erosion.
This job is too big for any government or any party. It is up to parliament to deal with it. I should1 like to point out to the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, who represent the government and the people of Canada, that we have many millions of dollars at stake. Both our trans-Canada railways, one publicly-owned and the other privately-owned, have a lot at stake. We have a big stake in the privately-owned railway, although we do not own it. The whole of Canada has a stake in these railways. The trans-Canada highway and the transcontinental telegraph lines are affected by these floods. The whole economy and the whole outlook have changed since the act was brought into being. Surely it should be apparent to everyone that no municipality or municipal government is in a financial position to guard against and prevent river bank erosion.
I am not an engineer, but I personally believe that the answer to erosion on the Fraser river bank is dredging. Ever since I have been a member of the house I have urged upon the minister the necessity of acquiring adequate dredging equipment. The only equipment we have now to prevent river bank erosion is one obsolete dredge which is forty years old. Its entire time is taken up in the port of Westminster and at the mouth of the Fraser valley. That is the only dredging equipment we have available.
I must admit that we 'have had certain small grants of $3,000, $5,000, and $8,000 in this connection, but it is a mere pittance. The work that it could do could be washed away in twenty minutes. It is time that the parliament of Canada looked at river bank erosion in the Fraser valley. It is a national problem and one that must be worked out. Some system of engineering should be worked out, not locally, so far as the Fraser river is concerned. A commission should be set up at once with complete authority as to diking, channeling, clearing and preventing river bank erosion on the Fraser river.
I urge the minister to take steps tonight. I hope that this session of parliament will be concluded by midnight. Before prorogation adequate funds should be voted to provide for ample dredging. A country with the wealth of Canada, and with what we have at stake, should be able to secure adequate dredging equipment to do the work. Any country that can spend $10,000,000 a day on destruction can surely find a few million dollars to prevent river bank erosion.

speechtext:
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a matter of serious concern to some 20.000 of my constituents living along the banks of the Columbia river or the Arrow lakes. It is of particularly serious concern at this time because of the damage occasioned by the recent floods, and the hope that something of a permanent nature will be done to prevent the recurrence of such damage.
A great part of the damage done in my constituency was done near the city of Trail, one of the greatest industrial communities in Canada. In addition to that, all the scattered communities and scattered farms along the shores of the Arrow lakes suffered damage to a greater or lesser extent. I am fully aware of the terms of the agreement between the dominion government and the provincial government with reference to assistance to the Fraser valley area, and that that area has been termed an area of national disaster, and that so far as rehabilitation is concerned the province has agreed to look after any difficulties in other parts of the province. That is not the aspect of the question that I wish to deal with. I wish to deal with the long-term approach to the regulation and control of these large rivers to prevent future flooding.
I am well acquainted with the Columbia river, which is the greatest river in British Columbia, because I have lived on its shores for forty-three years. My property is on its shores. In order to give the minister a fair picture-and I want to be as brief as possible 

I shall deal with a report I have here from 5849-385i
the city engineer of Trail, a report which outlines the damage and makes certain proposals. I have no exact knowledge of the damage in the upper parts of the river or in the Arrow lakes, but I stress this because it has a particular significance for the city of Trail, and I think the recommendation is an excellent one, certainly, which if acted upon, will protect a very important industrial community in Canada either in peace or war.
Prompt and aggressive measures were taken by the city of Trail and the Consolidated Mining and Smelling Company of Canada Limited to combat and control Columbia river flood and overflow of its banks into the city from the period May 31 to June 15.
Emergency building of temporary dikes and fills was continually maintained twenty-four hours a day, bringing to bear every available resource of men and equipment to protect life and property. In that respect I want to say that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada Limited was most generous in placing at the disposal of the committee its crews, equipment and engineering staff. Approximately a mile and a half of dikes and protective work were built in this time, including hauling and dumping at least 100,000 cubic yards of sand and gravel for fills and support of temporary dikes, including hauling and constructing timber work, using 60,000 board feet of material. Installation of relief sewers including seven pumping stations, pumping sewage through steel mains on surface to river by this method. The total joint expenditure incurred to date by the city of Trail and the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada Limited is $125,000. Of this sum the city's share has been agreed on as $50,000. That figure of costs does not include the voluntary work.

I am speaking now on behalf of the city of Trail, and I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the following factors. The fill material now in place on the ground could be used to very great economic advantage if joint government action were taken immediately to provide protective measures for the future, to forestall and prevent a recurrence of this ruinous condition.
It is believed that in the memory of present inhabitants of the area floods run in cycles. That is to say, there was in past years a series of successive very high- water conditions; this may very well happen again, possibly next year, and the people of that district and those engaged in the industry

 very important industry too, producing as it did last year nearly 1100 million worth of industrial products-believe that this is the opportune time to start preventive action in order to obviate a recurrence of the difficulty. The suggestion is made that 100,000 cubic yards of fill material now in place could be used by the dominion government in the permanent work to prevent a recurrence of floods, particularly along the waterfront, on both banks of the river at Trail.
Therefore I urge upon the -minister, particularly having heard that he sent one of his best engineers to British Columbia, to ask that engineer to visit Trail to see what can be done to use this 100,000 yardis of material for permanent improvement with a vie-w to preventing a recurrence of the difficulties that we have had in the last year.
In addition I would suggest that the department make a survey of the Columbia river from the international boundary to its source in order to see what should be done to prevent a recurrence of flood damage at various points.

speechtext:
Going through the estimates of the Department of Public Works for 194849 and the supplementaries, I find that the minister is asking the house for some $84,000,000 for his department, which is about $7 per capita for the people of Canada. Because I am concerned with the distribution of these funds across Canada, I was especially interested in the extent to which money was to be spent in my own province. I notice that, including the supplementaries, the Department of Public Works is spending there some 8620,000 this year. That works out to about 70 cents per capita in Saskatchewan or one tenth of the amount that is being expended on the average across the dominion. I do not want the minister to run away with the idea that we have no problems that cannot usefully be the duty of the public works department of Canada to do something about. It is for that reason that I wish to speak for a few minutes about problems that should be the concern of his department, some of which I have from time to time casually discussed with the minister. I want to mention two with regard to the southern part of Saskatchewan and Regina specifically.
We have in the city of Regina, for example, a number of buildings owned by the government of Canada, one of which is particularly attractive and ornate, and is called the federal building. But the departments of the Canadian government are housed and scattered in many privately-owned buildings throughout the city. I think possibly that condition applies to governments generally. They seem to have no particular scheme whereby they concentrate public buildings, either for efficient administration or for their more facile use by the public which has business with the government. It would seem to me that in the public works department, in all major centres where it is necessary to occupy extensive floor space, some sort of over-all planning might be adopted to house government departments either in a single building, or in a group of buildings convenient to traffic but forming a unit apart from the rest of the business district of the city concerned. Unfortunately, all our chambers of commerce lobby all senior governments. When there is a likelihood of a public building making its appearance in some portion of the country, they lobby for it in their particular city. I realize that situation applies, and I sympathize with the minister and the department for sometimes being put under a form of local patriotic pressure which is not always in keeping with the best distribution of the public services. However, that has gone on for decades and undoubtedly it will continue to do so. But I believe that functional planning of the buildings that will house the ever-increasing number of public services is necessary in all cities. Certainly that statement applies in special measure to my city of Regina. Last year, for example, a number of us went to the minister with respect to the taking over of a building that housed the Department, of Commerce offices. While we were negotiating with the government to do something about acquiring the building, it was

sold under their noses. There is the factor
*f delay in all these matters. I trust the govrnment or the minister will take cognizance of representations to plan the future development of public buildings.
I have another instance that concerns us in the southern part of Saskatchewan. I refer to the matter of water supply for cities in drought areas or in dry farming areas. This should concern our senior governments, because the senior governments in their buildings also use the services such as that of water. Saskatchewan, we have hit a delayed acquiescence from government departments. I do hope that when delegations from my city come to the government asking, as they are going to do, for sympathetic consideration in respect of increased (water reservoirs to help that city the Minister of Public Works, partly because the servicing of government buildings is involved, will give sympathetic consideration to the representations .made. I should like to ask the minister to say a word with regard to the wages paid to women cleaners, particularly in Winnipeg. As the minister knows, I have drawn this matter to his attention a number of times during the past few years. I want to thank him once again for the attention that he has given to my requests and for the successful representations that he has made in times past on behalf of these women. The points that I have drawn to his attention at times have been of an administrative nature, while on other occasions I have raised the question of holidays with pay and the important question of wage rates.
Some two or three years ago the minister was successful in persuading the proper authorities to agree to allow one week's holidays with pay for these women. They now receive six days' sick leave in a year, and this is not deducted from their holidays as was the case a few years ago. In years gone by there have been acceptable increases in the wages paid to these women, but I believe it is nearly two years since they have received any increase. In the meantime the cost of living has been going up and is bearing heavily upon them. They have also been conscious of the fact that other government employees in Winnipeg and throughout the country have received increases, and they have dared to hope that, through the months when increases were being announced, there would soon be an increase for them. But, as I said a moment ago, no increase has come through, their last increase being nearly two years ago. I ask the minister to give the same serious and sympathetic consideration to this matter that he has given in the past to the other matters I have brought before him concerning this group of women.
I do not wish to speak to the exclusion of women working in public buildings in other cities. Local conditions vary as between city and city and as to the hours that these women have to put in. I know the situation in Winnipeg and the women involved, and I submit to the minister that their case is deserving. These women do not work just two or three hours in the morning. I think they work seven hours a day for five, five and a half or perhaps six days a week. In other words, they have a full-time job. I think the time has come when they should be considered as being on a par with other government employees and given an increase in wages to meet the increased cost of living.

Secondly there is an increase in the allotment for materials and supplies because of increased cost of materials and labour, and due to the provision now being made in this allotment for alterations, partitions, improvement to lighting, et cetera, required in connection with the allocation of accommodation for all the departments in the various buildings in Ottawa. The net increase is $1,795,493.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: An increase of more than 25 per cent. What is the reason for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: There are two reasons. First of all, we are making more repairs to our buildings, which were sorely neglected in the war years; secondly, there has been an increase in the price of the materials themselves.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
With reference to many of these items, I feel myself in the position of a school boy returning home from school

Supply-Public Works
and telling his parents that he has forgotten to bring home his report. I have to ask some questions on these estimates, so that I can answer my electors when they call upon me and ask me about them. Item 330 amounts to $8,612,478 for maintenance and operation of public buildings and grounds, other than at Ottawa. I notice that for 25 per cent of this item, amounting to $2,109,944, there are no details. That seems to be customary in all the estimates that come before us, but this is quite a large amount.
Another matter I wish to refer to is the rental of public buildings by Ottawa departments in the city of Charlottetown. May I have a breakdown of that? How many buildings are rented? Has the department decided to erect a large building of their own in Charlottetown to take care of the different departments that are now occupying rented buildings?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
The only building rented in Charlottetown is for the wartime prices and trade board. It is rented from a Mr. Chapel at an annual rental of $1,500. All the other offices are located in buildings belonging to the federal government.
The second question was as to whether there was an estimate for the erection of a public building in Charlottetown. A site has not been purchased. We are inquiring into the best site. Probably the hon. member for Queens will be consulted. When we have the site we shall prepare the plans for that building.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: You have agreed on a location and site?

Mr. MoLURE: Is that site to be purchased by the federal government, by the provincial government, or by the city of Charlottetown?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: If it is to be a federal building it will be purchased by the federal government.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I believe the minister was ready to make a statement in reply to my representation on item 328. We are still in the same general field. Perhaps he might say something now.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
Yes. I shall explain to the hon. member the procedure with reference to revisions of salaries or wages of charwomen. A survey is made in every part of the country, and we try to meet the prices in the locality which are paid by private
industry. Then we make a recommendation to the labour department. They themselves, with the officials in the different departments, make a report and approve or disapprove our recommendation or modify it. When the hon. gentleman brought the Winnipeg case to my attention I asked for a report and found that about two weeks before that we had asked the labour department for an increase for the charwomen working all day. I believe it is six hours a day. I have not yet had a report from the labour department. When it comes in, it is submitted to treasury which passes final judgment on the matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that his department asked the labour department for an increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: We recommended an increase in this case to meet the wages paid locally to that class of employees in Winnipeg.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Was consideration given to the matter of lengthening the holiday period?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: That has not been studied lately. As the hon. member mentioned, we did give holidays and sick leave, but I have not heard that it has been reconsidered lately.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I would hope that the department would reconsider it. I do happen to know that these women do not particularly like the use of the word "char". It would seem to me that, since men doing comparable work are called cleaners, or sometimes men cleaners, we might meet the point and actually change the name of the women to women cleaners. It is perfectly honourable work. My own mother was a domestic servant, and I am not ashamed'-indeed I am proud- of people who do this kind of work, but they do have some feeling about it. One item here covers harbours and rivers generally, and I think I should refer again to Rustico harbour where protection is needed for the lighthouse property, the fishermen's houses and their equipment, such as boats and stages. This whole harbour is now threatened whenever a heavy storm comes up. Representations have been made to the minister from time to time and at least twice efforts have been made to put up a jigsaw breastwork as a protection. When the seas are very heavy the expenditure is just a waste of money. Ten or twelve thousand dollars have been spent there within the last two years and this amount is not worth ten cents as a protection for that beach. Some piles should be driven in there and a strong wall built. That work would have to be done only once. The sand would then collect inside of it and form a breastwork itself.
If the engineers were instructed to look into this matter carefully you would not be wasting $5,000 or $10,000 annually putting in the jigsaw affairs you put in there, which provide in a storm no more protection than a tencent article. Just an ordinary storm would wash the whole thing away. It would throw it up on the bank and, if the storm continued, the whole beach and all the dwelling houses would be swept away. This is a serious enough matter for some good engineers to look into it.
I sent the minister a copy of the plan of how the work should be done. That plan originated from fishermen who had lived there all their lives. One more storm like the one we had last fall-and it was not particularly severe-and you can say good-bye to your lighthouses as well as to the dwellings there. I serve notice on the government that they will be responsible to the fishermen for the
loss of their property, because representations have been made to the government.

speechtext:
This morning the Minister of Public Works was furnished with valuable information about the waters of our lakes and rivers from some members who reside inland in this dominion. While I listened to them, I thought of the words of a maritime poet:
Smile, ye inland lakes and rivers;
Flush, ye mountains in the dawn;
But my roving heart is ever
WTith tire ships of grey Saint John.
Now that we have returned in these estimates to the lonely sea and sky, I should like to say a word or two on behalf of some fishermen in the constituency I have the honour to represent. I wish to direct the minister's attention to one matter, and one matter only, and/ that is the condition of the wharf at Lorneville in the county of Saint John. A year or so ago, one summer day I sat on the beach at that village talking with a fisherman who was repairing his boat, and in the course of the conversation he said to me, "You know, I feel more at home on the water than I do on the land." I had never heard a man express that point of view before; afterwards I asked one or two men in the village who go out fishing what they thought about it, and they said:	"Most of
us fish, two men in a boat. We start off in the late afternoon, drift all night, and come back in the morning. Some days when it is foggy and rough many of the boys say, we are not going out tonight, but this man always went out in his boat alone, no matter how dirty the weather". He felt more at home on the water than on the land.
Supply-Public Works

The condition of the wharf in that fishing village is deplorable. There is no wharf left. I received a letter from the minister of the main church in that village a year or so ago, asking if something could not be done about the wharf, and I have had other applications about it. I have taken this matter up with the minister and his department at different times, and) in January, 1946, I received a tetter from the acting minister, notifying me that consideration was being given' to this wharf and that the possibility of a new wharf being constructed was under study. The wharf is all gone now, and that is a great handicap to the fishermen. I again bring the condition of that wharf to the attention of the minister and trust that he will give it his further consideration.
I should like to know just what is the present position with respect to the wharf and breakwater at Chance Harbour, a small fishing village. The wharf was badlly in need of repairs, and a year or so ago some money was voted to restore the wharf and breakwater. What is the position at Chance Harbour now?
In conclusion, I want to thank the minister for the dredging done at Dipper Harbour. Dredging was badly needed there. It has been done and it has proved of great service to the fishermen in taking their boats in and out and in moving what they call their cars, which are large wooden boxes which float in the water and in which they keep their lobsters.
Mr. FOURNIER, (Hull): I cannot make any promise, but I have told my officials that I should like to have these two projects studied. I should like to see a report on the conditions at Lomeville and Chance Harbour, and if they are as described by the hon. member he may be sure that I personally will see that something is done.

Supply-Public Works
ferry service across the lake would be of great interest to quite a large territory north of that port. ' .Mr. GREEN: The hon. member for Fraser Valley was not in the house when the minister gave the details. The minister said that dredging was all to be done below New Westminster.

That will be taken up under the vote in the name of the Minister of Finance. When we reach that I shall discuss flood conditions. So far as I can see, no item is provided for dredging the Fraser river from the New Westminster bridge eastward as far as you want to go. One may say the Mission bridge or above Hope or Rosedale. The minister talked about keeping the navigable part of the river in the condition it was before the floods. That is entirely out. I informed the minister, and am prepared to prove it by pictures, by affidavits or by anything else he wishes, that that is not good enough.
I shall mention two districts, Matsqui island and McDonald bar. You can practically wade across the famous Fraser river. I maintain that no item has been provided in either the main estimates or the supplementary estimates for the dredging of that channel. No provision has been made, so far as I can find, in the main estimates, the supplementary estimates or the further supplementary estimates, to provide equipment for that service. I am asking the minister to give me an assurance that he will make a proper recommendation to the government in this matter.
I frankly admit that neither the minister nor anyone else can state now what amount will be required; but on behalf of the people

whom I represent, the people who are most affected, I ask the minister to give me an assurance that a recommendation will be made to the government that McDonald bar, Calamity Point and the Matsqui island bar will be dredged out; and not merely for the purpose of providing navigation, because no navigation has been possible for the past fifteen years, owing to neglect on the part of the Department of Public Works, both federal and provincial. I would ask the minister to give me the assurance that further sums will be recommended. I cannot say how much will be required, and I do not think the minister can say at this moment what will be required, but I submit that he should tell this committee and assure me, as representing the people of that riding, that, by order in council if necessary, funds sufficient will be found to dredge this channel, in order to make it safe, not only for navigation but for the safety of the two trans-Canada railways, the trans-Canada highway and the whole economy of Canada. I think the minister should be in a position to give that assurance.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
I am not talking about flood damage or anything else of that description, but about dredging. Surely the minister can tell me this. What provision has been made to date to acquire suitable dredging equipment? You cannot acquire a dredge overnight. When we built the famous Sumas dike, which held, thanks to its erection under Dudley Barrow, who built it, we brought a dredge from the Panama canal. In the province of British Columbia, ever since 1940, the federal government has had one two-by-four dredge-I have forgotten the name; it is either the Samson or the King Edward- which is forty years old, which could only keep the port of New Westminster open. I have no objection to keeping that port open.
I see a vote for dredging in the port of Victoria. I have no objection to that, but what is the reason? It is for the great commercial interests. I can tell you that we had to rush dredges over from the Fraser river there during the war. The war is over and we can say these things now. The fact is that we had to rush dredges there in order to get into that dry dock. Those dredges were taken off the Fraser river.
I am surprised that the British Columbia members have not got up and demanded-not requested but demanded-that suitable dredging facilities be procured immediately for the great Fraser river from one end to the other.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I should like to raise a point with the minister. He can correct me if I am wrong, but I believe he said the idea was to restore the channel of the Fraser river to the condition it was in before the flood.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: God help us.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
If that is the statement, it is necessary to draw to the attention of the department the fact that, in the opinion of the majority of the people on the spot, that will not be sufficient. It has been pointed out by the hon. member for Fraser Valley that at one time the waters of the Fraser were navigable at a much higher position than they are today. That river is in a condition of geological maturity and it is silting up in all its upper reaches. As a consequence of that fact, the dangers of the flood menace, of which we have had experience recently, are due largely, or in part at any rate, to the failure to retain the
condition of the river, from the navigable point of view, as it was fifteen or twenty years ago.
