The minister could not but note this morning that there was a general feeling of humour in the house when he said that the government had not had time to consider the report. Most of us feel that the government has been considering what was in that report for a long time, even before the members of the committee had it.
I do feel that before this session comes to an end, whether it be tonight, tomorrow night or at some future sitting, the minister should make a statement about these matters. I hope he will not be worried over the way in which we have poked at the government because of divisions in its ranks and the difficulties they have had in changing policies without losing face, but that he will tell the house and the country what the government of Canada intends to do on the basis of the

Supply-Finance
financial recommendations contained in the report of the prices committee, which as I have said has already been approved by the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
As I said this morning, the report has been tabled only recently, and with the pressure of work in trying to bring the session to a close I was correct when I stated that the government has not yet had an opportunity to give full and careful consideration to the recommendations of the committee. maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
Like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I am surprised that the minister is not ready to tell us tonight everything he is prepared to do, but I suppose that is a way that ministers have. It used to be merely a means of raising money for the expenses of the various departments of government, but now it is far more than that. Now it goes very far into our ordinary lives in its efforts to control the economy of the country.
There has been a measure of reorganization in the department this year, I understand, a sort of splitting up of functions. Would the minister give us a brief statement on that, and lay some stress on what we call the regulatory side and the extent to which the department steps into the economy of the country. I would ask the minister to say something in particular as to the relations of this department with the Bank of Canada and other important bodies in the nation, but banks chiefly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
There has been no reorganization of the department this year. Last year there was some reorganization involving what I might call the top executive branch. Three assistant deputy ministers were appointed last
year, and there was a rearrangement of the branches, the directorates and so on. But all that was done last year, and there has been no change made this year. The estimate for this year shows an increase of $65,901 over last year.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: It was the reorganization made last year that I thought the minister might speak about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
It was actually made before I brought in my main estimate last year. The reorganization consisted of Mr. Kenneth W. Taylor being appointed, if I might say so, senior assistant deputy minister, but because of the fact that Mr. Taylor is still continuing to serve as chairman of the wartime prices and trade board he has been able to devote only a portion of his time to the duties of assistant deputy minister of finance. Of course, as the committee is aware, he is also head of the emergency import control division, which is under the direction of the Minister of Finance. One other assistant deputy minister who was appointed last year was Doctor Eaton, who for some time had been head of the taxation branch of the department. He also was given the status of a deputy minister, but is still continuing to perform the duties of head of the taxation branch. Mr. R. B. Bryce, who had been one of the senior officers of the department, was made assistant deputy minister. Mr. W. C. Ronson was made master of the mint. Since that time Mr. Bryce has been assistant deputy minister with particular responsibility for the treasury board side of the department. Mr. M. W. Sharp, who had been in the department for many years, is director of the economic policy division. Mr. Deutsch, who is known to a good many members of the committee, is: head of the commercial branch. These were-the principal-well, they were not changes, they were actually giving to these very valuable officers of the department a status which I think was well merited as a result of the work which they had been performing during the war years. There has been no fundamental; change in the organization of the department, except, as I say, to recognize the particular responsibilities of those who were in it.
There has been no substantial increase in the administrative cost. The increase is $65,006 odd. All of that is substantially to provide for various salary and statutory increases. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: May I take just a moment longer to get clear, if I can, the significance of the minister's answers to my questions a moment ago. Re Excise Tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I am quile aware, as are hon. members of this house, that there is a great state of confusion and uncertainty as to what is going to happen in connection with this excise tax. maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:

The government started the new fiscal year with a bang, piling up a surplus of $255,261,473 in the first two months of operations.

At the corresponding date last year the government had a surplus of $202,195,966.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: It is $2,000,000 greater.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I do not indulge in prophecy, and the estimates of this year were prepared on the most careful and honest basis possible. What has been overlooked in all this talk about extra excise taxes that were put on is the fact that the excise taxes put on consisted of an additional tax on automobiles, radios and certain household appliances such as curling irons and toasters.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Washing machines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: No; it was not imposed on those.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
It was never put on. It was announced at first but never imposed. The tax was imposed on miscellaneous electrical appliances and refrigerators. At the same time, a fact that has never been emphasized in this house, we removed the tax from the domestic use of electricity, which affects every household, and we took off the duties that had been levied on tea and coffee, and the revenue equivalents of these taxes were very close to the estimated yield from the taxes imposed.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

I wish to touch upon the matter raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The people, however, are worrying about the codt of living. That is the question that is worrying them and they cannot get very much satisfaction from the answer which the Minister of Finance gave the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I would point out to the minister, if it needs pointing out to him, that this question of the cost of living is important, and the people are expecting some assurance that the report which was approved here yesterday, and the recommendations or proposals that were made, mean something, that they

That word "consideration" has so many barnacles on it that you cannot see the word, and that kind of thing is mighty dangerous at this time. maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Will the minister give a brief explanation of the regulations under which Canadian securities owned in Britain can be purchased in Britain for the purpose of obtaining Canadian currency to invest in industry in this country? Under what conditions can that be done, what type of securities must be purchased, and to what use can the money be put in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
I take it my hon. friend is referring to the use of the proceeds of sale of Canadian securities owned by British residents for the purpose of investment in Canada. The situation there is this. As the committee is aware, under the agreement which was entered into with the United Kingdom government, and confirmed by an act of this house, relating to the non-interest bearing loan from Canada to the United Kingdom, it was provided that when dollar securities held by residents of the United Kingdom were sold or redeemed, the proceeds of sale or redemption would be used to reduce the amount of the non-interest bearing loan. That was the general provision in the agreement. In December 1946 it was agreed between the two governments that the proceeds of such sales could be used for direct investment in Canada. That is to say, if United Kingdom residents were anxious to establish plants in Canada to manufacture some commodity here, the proceeds of sale of Canadian securities held by residents of the

Supply-Finance
United Kingdom-sale or redemption.-instead of being used to pay on the loan immediately, could be used in direct investment in Canada. In other words, the practical effect of that was that a negotiable security, if I might put it that way, could be converted into plant in Canada. The asset would still be in Canada, but it would take the form of some productive asset here. That arrangement has been in effect since December, 1946, I think, and that is the position today. There is no change from that position. There has not been a great deal of investment so far in virtue of that provision, but it is available for those who wish to make use of it.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Does that apply only to British residents, or does it apply to other people as well? That is, can people other than British residents ibuy these Canadian securities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: That applies only to British residents, because those securities are those which have been registered by British residents with the Bank of England in London, and are under the control of the British treasury. It is perfectly true, of course, that anybody can purchase those securities; but the proceeds of the sale of the securities owned iby residents of the United Kingdom must either be used to pay off the non-interest bearing loan or be re-invested ini various investments in Canada, as I have indicated.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Are the proceeds being used for the purpose of building plants in this country, or is it not a fact that in some cases they are being used for the purchase of existing plants which, of course, would be far more inflationary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: They are supposed to be used only for the actual building of plants or the extension of existing plants.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Will the minister state if the government exercises some control in the matter? Let us assume that the British owner of the security wished to build a plant to make a commodity which is in surplus production and which would be doomed to failure. Would the government exercise any control in a situation of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
No. We do not attempt to exercise control over the nature of the enterprise that the British manufacturer or industrialist wants to establish in Canada. We believe in free enterprise, of course; and if he wants to switch from a negotiable security, such as the bonds of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power or Canadian Pacific, or something like that, to a plant in Ottawa, Toronto or
somewhere else, we are glad to have him do so, because that increases the productive facilities of Canada. The security must be sold or must be redeemed; that is what I meant when I said "switched."

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I never heard of that agreement until about a month ago. Was the negotiation made public before then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I cannot say.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
It was known to the
minister, of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: We did not put any advertisements about it in the paper, but I think it has been known since early in the spring of 1947. Obviously the persons who are entitled to avail themselves of it are residents of the United Kingdom who want to establish plants here in Canada. Canadians have no control over that.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: It is in the nature of a concession to them, is it not? Until this agreement was entered into, of which I in my ignorance had no knowledge until the other day, the proceeds from the sale of that type of security which the minister has mentioned were applied, automatically almost, against the noninterest bearing loan. That is the fact, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: And now they may be diverted to other uses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: They may be converted into another type of investment, yes. We still have the asset here in Canada as a security against our loan.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: That is true; but it is not a realization upon the security which you hold, or it is not a payment on account of the obligation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Of course, as my hon. friend knows, the value of the securities held by residents of the United Kingdom in dollar securities is substantially in excess of the noninterest bearing loan.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I think the reason this matter has come up is the fact that the Financial Post gave it a great deal of publicity about a month or two ago. I was wondering what about Canadians who had capital in England or funds in England. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
In the case of Canadians who have securities in England they own sterling securities. If those were to be sold, they would

realize sterling. In order to make those available for investment in Canada, the British treasury would have to provide Canadian dollars; and I doubt very much if they would be willing to do that.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I wish to ask one question of the minister. I understood him to say that these funds produced in the manner indicated were to be invested in Canada only in new buildings, not in existing enterprises.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Or in the extension of existing ones.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: That struck me as odd, because I thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce was now playing down new construction, and it seems to me he should have done that long ago. If I am correct in thinking that, why would the policy be to insist that these funds should go into new construction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: There is a good deal of expansion going on here. As I say, the amount which has been availed of is small compared with the increased investments here. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
It is a matter that is within the control and discretion of the British
treasury. If a Canadian insurance company is willing to advance to a resident of the United Kingdom Canadian dollars against the security of sterling assets which that resident of the United Kingdom has in Great Britain, the transaction requires the consent of the British treasury, because the British resident is in effect undertaking at some future date to pay off the loan in Canadian dollars and is putting up as security sterling assets. If the British treasury is willing to agree to such a transaction we in Canada, broadly speaking, would welcome it.
The reason why it can be done is this. Insurance companies which have liabilities to meet in the United Kingdom in sterling are obliged to have sterling assets in order to meet them, and they may be quite ready to advance funds to a resident of the United Kingdom in Canada and take, as collateral, securities which are payable in sterling. That is the type of transaction, but it requires the consent of the British treasury, not the Canadian treasury, because Canadian dollars are not being put up by the Canadian exchange control. They are in effect being provided by the British exchange control. The Bank of England says in effect: We will allow you to assume an obligation payable in Canadian dollars and you pledge sterling securities to guarantee repayment. The consent of the British treasury is required because, if there were default, the British treasury would have to provide the Canadian dollars to meet the obligation.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: A Canadian company with a surplus of sterling, which many of them have, in view of the British exchange restrictions, will advance money to a British concern to erect a plant in Canada, which is a way of transferring a loan in sterling from the United Kingdom to Canada in Canadian dollars, and the debt is owed at all times to the insurance company. It is merely a means of transferring the debt from the sterling area to the Canadian area. The Canadian government has no objection to that, and in fact would welcome it. Is that it?

He provides the resident of the United Kingdom with a credit in a Canadian bank, upon which he can draw to pay for that plant. Of course he does not do that for fun, but takes some type of security, usually an assignment or a pledge of securities or cash. If he can use the sterling in the United Kingdom, so much the better. If the British exchange control, the Bank of England, is willing to allow the British treasury

to convert sterling in the United Kingdom into Canadian dollars we are delighted. They can nearly always find a person who wishes to use sterling. That is how these transactions can be arranged with the consent of the British treasury, if they are satisfied that it is advantageous to both parties, and apparently there is some indication that they are prepared to do so.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it would be wise on this occasion to give the events as they occurred. Some people seem to think we moved rather slowly. If we go over just as hurriedly as possible the events, the committee will be able to follow it more closely. On May 24 and 25 flood damages became serious. The water level at Mission rose to 18-82 feet. On May 26 the banks of Agassiz broke and flooded about a thousand acres of land. The water level at Mission rose to 21-6 feet. On May 27 Dewdney dike breaks. On May 28 Canadian Pacific railway main line washed out. First army troops called out. Messrs. Cruickshank. Fulton and Matthews draw-attention of House of Commons to gravity of situation. Mr. Claxton outlines steps being taken by Department of National Defence.
On May 29 last rail connection with east severed. Mr. E. R. Gillie, Red Cross chairman, is named as supreme commander of all flood disaster relief and aid. Three armed services set up a province-wide communications system with headquarters at Red Cross House, where all requests for aid will be cleared. Right Hon. C. D. Howe, visiting British Columbia, is
reported to have stated that British Columbia floods had reached the proportions of a national disaster and that the federal government was prepared to give all assistance possible.
On May 30 Fraser river reaches highest point since 1894 at Hell's Gate, 107 feet.
On May 31 Premier Johnson proclaims a state of emergency with Colonel Snow, area commander of the Canadian army, being authorized to co-ordinate all flood control and relief activities. Flood relief fund started with $1,000,000 as objective. Prime Minister Mackenzie King states in the House of Commons that the responsibility for financial assistance to those suffering from floods and similar disasters of nature lies with provincial governments and local communities as well as with non-governmental organizations such as the Red Cross. Mr. King pointed out that any federal government financial assistance would only be made in the light of representations by the provincial governments concerned.
On June 1 Sumas prairie dike breaks at. Connor. Mission gauge rises to 24-45 feet. Prime Minister Mackenzie King informs the House of Commons that his statement of the previous day referred only to the question of direct financial assistance. He pointed out that from the beginning of the floods the dominion government had been rendering assistance on a considerable scale in other ways, such as army, et cetera. Mr. Claxton advises the house further measures being taken by the Royal Canadian Navy, Canadian Army and Royal Canadian Air Force.
On June 3 Prime Minister King announces that the federal government is prepared to assist the province financially, not only in meeting the expenditures required for immediate relief but also in meeting the costs of rehabilitation and restoration. Mr. King also announces the formation of the Fraser river relief and rehabilitation commission to have general supervision over the entire situation. Mr. Claxton advises the house that army personnel actively participating in disaster work total 1,482.
On June 4 the Prime Minister announced that Major General B. M. Hoffmeister will be dominion government's representative on Fraser valley relief and rehabilitation commission. Finance Minister Abbott advises-the house that prices board has been authorized to pay a subsidy of up to six cents a pound on butter flown into the flood areas -from Calgary and Edmonton.
On June 6 Mr. St. Laurent, while visiting British Columbia, is reported to have stated that the relief for British Columbia flood victims would not be delayed by waiting to
Supply-Finance

determine the extent of the flood damage. He said that the people were entitled to know that everything reasonable would be done and would be done expeditiously. Record June temperatures continue to melt snow and hasten run-off.
On June 9 Prime Minister Mackenzie King announces the basis on which the dominion government will share the costs of relief and rehabilitation in the Fraser valley. Mr. Claxton advises the house that in addition to naval and air force personnel engaged in the flood area there are also 1,226 active and 1,359 reserve army personnel, with another 500 members active force on the way from the prairie command.
On June 10 flood level at Mission reaches a new high of 24-62 feet.
On June 11 evacuation of Sumas prairie region nears completion.
On June 14 Mr. Sinclair requests details on government's program for rehabilitation.
On June 17 Premier Johnson announces that homes and farms in Fraser valley flood regions will be restored. Work to be carried out by four departments of the provincial government.
On June 18 first transcontinental train in eighteen days arrives in Vancouver from the east.
On June 25 Prime Minister Mackenzie King advises the House of Commons that the dominion government's financial contribution in respect of the Fraser valley disaster would consist of a grant to the province of $5,000,000 for relief and rehabilitation, and the sharing, to the extent of 75 per cent, in the cost of repairing, strengthening and reconstructing the dikes and removing water and debris from flooded land. The Prime Minister also announced the formation of the Fraser valley diking board to carry out this work. That brings us up to June 25, and I have here a statement that came in today with regard to the condition.
The information that we have received here today indicates that the flood waters are now dropping about six inches in each twenty-four hour period, and that by tomorrow morning the level of the water at the gauge at Mission will be down to the 18-foot mark, which has been taken as terminating the emergency period. As a consequence, the attorney general of the province last night, after consulting Mr. Dixon, who is the provincial government engineer on dikes, and Mr. Good-speed, the dominion government engineer, who went to that area about the 19th of the month, who are now to be responsible for the operation on dikes, and the flood control comfMr. Mayhew.]
mittee, signed a declaration stating that the emergency is now ended and that the services of the active militia are no longer required in aid of the civilian power.
Following the declaration, the national defence authorities have arranged for the responsibility of the military authorities to be handed over entirely to the existing civilian authorities, or those which have been set up for the purpose of relief and rehabilitation on the one hand by the province, and for the work on dikes by the dominion and the provincial government jointly.
The military forces are to be withdrawn from the area this week, commencing tomorrow, and it is expected that the movement will be completed as soon as the transportation companies can provide the necessary facilities.
With the ending of the emergency, the flood control committee originally set up by the province held its final meeting, but will remain available for consultation. The active direction of the continuing work on relief and rehabilitation will be carried out by the provincial authorities, who have taken over the work by agreement, as explained in the announcements in the past ten days.
This work is under the immediate direction of Mr. W. L. Macken and Colonel D'Arcy Baldwin. These men are appointed by the provincial government to work on repairs and reconstruction of dikes, and the removing of water from the flooded lands is now being carried on under the immediate direction of Mr. Bruce Dixon and Mr. Goodspeed, pending the establishment of (the proposed Fraser valley diking board. Work is at present going forward on the agreement under which the board will be established. The personnel has been agreed upon and, I understand, will be announced later this evening. This review makes it evident that the emergency is now over and that the arrangements which have been worked out between the provincial government and this government have taken effect quickly and smoothly. It is a matter for gratification that the province and the dominion have been able to reach agreement so quickly in this urgent matter.
I cannot let this opportunity pass, however, without drawing to the attention of the committee the vital role which the defence forces of this country have played in dealing with this emergency. All three services provided help quickly and effectively. At one time as many as 3,000 members of the active and reserve army forces were engaged in evacuation, relief, protection of dikes and flood control. From all sides and all sources, there has

Supply-Finance
been a general appreciation of the excellent work which the services have done in this emergency.
That brings us up to the present time. So far as the work is going, apparently the emergency is pretty well over. This does not mean that the work is by any means over. It is really just beginning. The Prime Minister, on June 26, gave a statement to the house on the genera! agreement. At the same time the Premier of British Columbia made a statement in Victoria. I have received this wire from Premier Johnson, dated June 25:
Apart from press statement issued on dominion provincial arrangements on Fraser valley flood separate statement was given out today stating that the province was assuming full responsibility for flood damage elsewhere in t'he province outside of the Fraser valley area and that Honourable E. T. Kenney was making a tour of these areas with a view to reporting his recommendations to the government so that action can be taken in connection therewith.
Byron I. Johnson, Premier of British Columbia.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that you will allow the release to the press, which has now appeared in the newspapers, to go on the record. It is lengthy, but it has already been reported and I should like to have it on Hansard, because it is complementary to the statement made by the Prime Minister in this house, and the two together form the agreement. With the permission of the committee, I would ask that it be put on the record without being read.

speechtext:
I will hand it to Hansard.
Canadian Pacific Telegraphs Victoria, B.C'.. June 25 Hon. R. W. Mayhew Minister of Fisheries, Ottawa.
Following is text of press statement issued by me today:
"Premier Byron Johnson today confirmed the conclusion of his negotiations with the federal authorities for tlieir participation in sharing responsibilities in connection with the Fraser valley flood, which was proclaimed a national disaster. The arrangement, Premier Johnson stated, is as follows:
1.	The dominion government will make an outright grant of $5,000,000 to the provincial government to cover the dominion's share of temporary emergency relief as well as the financial liability for measures of rehabilitation which the government of Canada agreed to accept as announced by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons on June 9.
2.	The provincial government will assume full responsibility for immediate relief and assisting in the general rehabilitation of homes, farm buildings and damage sustained by provincial and municipal property.
3.	The dominion government will set up a Fraser valley diking authority for the purpose of repairing the dikes, removing water from inundated areas, removing debris and for the purpose of completely reconstructing the entire diking system so that wherever it is humanly possible a recurrence of the disastrous floods may be avoided. The cost of this work will be shared on the basis of 75 per cent by the dominion government and 25 per cent by the provincial government.
4.	Cost of protecting the dikes and combating the flood will be shared on the following basis: 75 per cent by the dominion government and 25 per cent by the provincial government.
The fund being raised by the B.C. flood relief fund committee is rapidly approaching the $2,000,000 mark. This fund is under the complete control of the committee which has organized it. It is understood that they have asked rlie Canadian Red Cross Society to administer the proceeds of public subscriptions for them for the purpose of providing personal belongings lost in the flood, the replacement or repair of essential household furnishings, food and other necessities which may be urgently needed.
In connection with the diking work the federal government will appoint a top-ranking administrator to head the diking authority. Working with this authority will be Mr. Bruce Dixon, provincial diking commissioner who has been appointed by the provincial government as its representative. F. G. Goodspeed, chief engineer of the dominion public works department, will be the federal representative.
"Mr. Dixon," the premier stated, "has a thorough knowledge of the Fraser valley diking system and has carried out excellent work in connection with the combating of the flood during the present crisis. His knowledge in this respect should be of inestimable value to the Fraser valley diking authority."
The rehabilitation work will be undertaken by a provincial commission comprising two members, namely, Mr. W. L. Macken and Colonel D'Arcy Baldwin, both of whom hare done outstanding work during the past five weeks in connection with fighting tile flood in the Chilliwack area.
"The government, in appointing Mr. Macken and Colonel Baldwin to the provincial commission on Fraser valley rehabilitation, did so because of tehir administrative and organizing ability," the premier stated.
"Mr. Macken and Colonel Baldwin will supervise the work of the entire valley and will have authority to expend such sums as are required to assist owners of property in their efforts to rehabilitate their homes and farm buildings," the premier stated.
"It is the government's desire that every assistance shall be given, but it is expected that every initiative willl be shown by the owners in recovering and restoring their damaged property," the premier continued.
The municipal authorities have been asked b.v Honourable R. C. MacDonald, minister of municipal affairs, to render the fullest co-operation and assistance to the commission in this work.
In commenting upon the final arrangements that have been made between the dominion and the province, Premier Johnson stated that he was most gratified with the wholehearted co-operation and sympathetic consideration he had received from the federal authorities in arriving at the arrangements already outlined.
Supply-Finance

He pointed out that the major task was that of reconstructing the dikes on a basis that would give the utmost sense of security to the people as far as human effort can go.
"No one can tell just what a river will do when it is on the rampage, but I can assure the citizens of British Columbia that, having discussed this work with the federal authorities, it^ is their clear understanding, even as it is mine, that the reconstruction work will be of such a character that the people's confidence in the protection of their property will be maintained and a sense of security established beyond that which they have enjoyed before," the premier asserted.
"I would also like to take this opportunity of expressing tile very deep gratitude of the government for the splendid volunteer service rendered by our provincial representative, the Honourable Erie W. Hamber, C.M.G., who worked so harmoniously and untiringly with Major General B. M. Hoffmeister, C.B., C.B.E., D.S.O., E.D., the dominion representative on the Fraser river relief and rehabilitation commission, which was established jointly by the dominion and provincial authorities in the early stages of the flood so that they could guide the two governments in taking such measures as were deemed necessary to meet the changing conditions of the time and to set up the necessary organization to undertake the work which was bound to follow the recession of the water. The work of Major General Hoffmeister and the Honourable Eric Hamber has come to a close and I think that I would be failing in my duty if I did not express on behalf of the government and people of British Columbia our warmest thanks for their endeavours," the premier stated.
Premier Johnson likewise expressed his sincere appreciation to Prime Minister Mackenzie King and the federal government for the splendid spirit of co-operation amd sympathetic understanding that has actuated the federal authorities in all their negotiations with the province in reaching a basis upon which to share financial responsibility in the costly undertakings imposed by the Fraser river calamity.
"In particular, I would like to mention the names of the Hon. R. W. Mayhew, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, the Hon. Douglas Abbott and the Hon. Brooke Claxton. ail of whom were ever willing to he of assistance and to relieve us of our great anxieties. My thanks go out alike to all those federal members who have been of assistance in this regard."
"Further I think the time has come, now that the waters are gradually receding, to express my heartfelt thanks to all of those persons who worked along the dikes and in organizing evacuation, emergency shelter, etc. Very many names and organizations come to my mind but it would be unfair to those who worked silently and courageously without thought of public recognition if I singled out any particular one. It was a great experience for me to witness the wonderful spirit of the people, the courage in the face of calamity and their indomitable will to overcome the frightful disaster which wreaked so much damage and caused so much *distress," the premier continued.
"I wish also to express the thanks of tihe citizens and the government for the very splen-

did work carried out by the Canadian Red Cross Society, the B.C. flood relief committee and the personnel of the three armed services," the premier concluded.
Byron Johnson.
A good deal of work had to be done, and these estimates are before the committee. No one can say they are accurate. In connection with them, a certain amount of common sense had to be exercised, and certainly no one was trying merely to get by with the least amount of money possible. The Canadian people demonstrated clearly, in their donations to the relief fund, which is now some $2,000,000, that they want a fairly reasonable agreement between the two governments. However I wish to make it clear that some of our own people had seen this area and realized that there had been a national disaster.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) visited the area himself and with him was the deputy minister of public works, Mr. Murphy. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) also visited the Fraser valley area, and so did the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg), and latterly the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent). All these gentlemen visited the area, and others who did so were the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair), the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) and myself. We made four separate trips over that area.
On one occasion I flew in a small plane, and we were able to fly at tree-top level so that we got a good view of the situation. I had never thought I would be guilty of so many stunts in the air as I performed on that occasion, but I did get a good view of what was happening and I can assure the committee that we were all agreed that it was a national disaster of the first order.
Perhaps another statement I should make here is with reference to a telegram which was received by the Minister of Finance from General Hoffmeister. It is the final telegram in this series.

It is dated the 25th of June and reads:
The statement made in the House of Commons today concerning the Fraser valley flood is very satisfactory and agrees in detail with the understanding here. It is the view of the commission that the statement finalizes the work of the commission particularly in view of the provincial government having already assumed full responsibility for rehabilitation of public and private property. In view of the foregoing it is therefore respectfully recommended that the

Supply-Finance
commission be dissolved forthwith; however if desirable to be available in an advisory capacity. There will not be any expenses submitted in connection with the administration of or in .any other respect of the commission. The utmost co-operation has been extended by the provincial government representatives of the dominion government BjC. area headquarters (army), the R.C.A.F. and members of the flood control .organizations all of which is gratefully acknowledged. E. W. Hamber concurs with all of the foregoing.
I think that concludes those statements. The first item in the supplementary estimates is 932, for 84,500,000. That item is the amount which we believe can be spent this year before March 31; that is the fiscal year of this government. It does not indicate that this is the total cost or our total participation in the diking to be done in that area.
The other item is 933, for 85,000,000. I will deal with it in only a few words. We had two choices. We had the choice of setting up several committees, all doing some part of the work within the area and working jointly with a similar number from the province. In the opinion of the committee and in the opinion of the subcommittee of the cabinet that was dealing with this matter, it would be much better if we could arrive at a lump sum and leave the entire obligation and opportunity of doing this job to the provincial government. It was difficult to set up a committee without losing time in the doing of it and without involving a great deal of expense. So far as the dominion government were concerned, we would have had to send people out from Ottawa. We would have had to send out representatives from the treasu^ board, the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Public Works and nearly every department of the government would have had to be represented in this. By doing it in this way, we were able to get action much quicker than would otherwies have been possible; and I am sure that it is a much tidier job all the way through than it would have been if we had tried to be in on every piece of work that was to be done. I think that probably explains the matter about as fully as I can at the present time.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
I listened with a great deal of interest to the British Columbia minister's explanation of the flood situation, past and present, in that province, 99 per cent of the effects of which flood happen to be in my riding. I appreciate his explanation. I only want to say to the government that possibly if some of the statements he has made tonight had been made two or three weeks ago, you would not have the unfortunate feeling you have in all parts of Canada, particularly
in British Columbia, and especially in the Fraser Valley riding which I have the honour to represent. In the dates the minister quoted, he did not mention that of May 28, about four o'clock in the afternoon when the member for Fraser Valley in this house said the flood situation was no longer a Fraser valley matter. I am sorry he did not mention that. I think he, as the minister from British Columbia, might have done so. About four o'clock on May 28, last, I said it was no longer a Fraser valley matter, but was a national matter. At that time I said that within twenty-four hours the trans-Canada railways would be out of action. I erred in that. Within ten hours they were out of action.
The Canadian National Railways, which the people of Canada, the taxpayers, own, is still out of action and will be out of action for some time to come. I am sorry the minister neglected to mention that fact. This flood situation has become such a national affair that even Pravda mentions it. We have heard a great deal of blame placed on the communists. I am surprised that even these floods were not blamed on them. I cannot read this in Russian, but I shall read a translation of what Pravda said. The minister, in his statement, apparently overlooked this. This is a news item from Pravda:
Canadian newspaper report that as a result of hot weather which caused intensive melting of snow in the mountains of British Columbia (Canada) over a period of two weeks, large floods have resulted. The rivers overflowed their shores and flooded many communities.
An hon. MEMBER; Are you reading in Russian?

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
If I could read it
in Russian, possibly the same people from Ontario could not even understand it in that language, when it concerned all Canada. To continue:
Fifty thousand acres of farm land were covered and over 9,000 population lost their homes. The railway lines between British Columbia and the rest of Canada were washed away, as well as the nail connections with the United States. The flood is continuing.
And the note I have says;
Date not known exactly, but two weeks after flood had reached a high point.
The reason I am mentioning this to you and through you, Mr. Chairman, to the committee, is that I said on May 28 that this was not a Fraser valley matter but was a national matter, as was recognized ten days later by the Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada when he stated that it was a national matter.
Supply-Finance

What would have happened if we had had an international incident during the interval? According to t'he press of yesterday, that great leader-a Conservative, if you like, but the greatest leader the British empire ever knew-Winston Churchill, said that nobody knew what might happen in the next two weeks. I want .to ask the minister and through him, the government, what would have happened if that incident had happened during the past two or three weeks when the Pacific coast, the direct route to Russia, was cut off from the rest of Canada? I hope I am not a warmonger, but I believe in facing realities; and I resent the fact that the minister from British Columbia overlooked what the member for Fraser Valley said on May 28, but quoted everybody else.
I want to go home like everyone. I do not believe in recriminations. What 'has happened, has happened. I firmly believe that this government has every intention of doing the right thing for the people of the Fraser valley and the people of British Columbia in all the flooded districts. I will tell you t'he reason why I believe they have that intention. It is that I believe the people of Canada as a whole would demand that any government do the right thing for their fellow citizens, who are victims of circumstances beyond their control.
The only thing is that I wish this cabinet, this government or the members of parliament had the time to observe some of the pictures I have. I should like to show the minister who introduced this estimate the house that I lived in, and I am not appealing for sympathy personally. I did not own the house. Though the farm land happens to be flooded, my house and barn are above high water. I should like to show the minister a picture of the house in which I spent the happiest years of my life. I spent the first three years of my married life in a house now flooded to the eaves. Yet the minister tells me that this token payment is representative of what the people of Canada want to do. The deputy minister tells me the record of assistance to the distressed countries of Europe; and I have no condemnation of that; I believe the people of my riding and I believe the people in my province agree with that. Speaking from memory, I believe we gave $124 million to the distressed people of Europe. In one vote alone we gave $5,000,000. Yet I am told that this is the best we can do to rehabilitate some 2,500 farms that are flooded out right up to the eaves, when many of the buildings have floated away, as well as every bit of the people's furniture.

This represents the lifelong savings of people, many of whom are sixty-five or seventy years of age. These people are flooded out, ruined. But, in the great generosity of the people of Canada we can find for them $5,000,000, less, of course, what we have advanced to the army, as has been brought out by the hon. member for Vancouver South! Why, in one vote alone -and I do not begrudge it at all-in one vote alone for the distressed peoples in Europe we can vote $5,000,000. But does anyone tell me that the people of Canada in their generosity can vote only $5,000,000 to rehabilitate some
2.500	homes, homes which are completely ruined, completely lost, homes where there will be no crops for one, two or three years, homes where the life savings will be gone? That the generosity of the people of Canada goes only to the extent of $5,000,000 does not make any sense to me; and I do not think it makes any sense to the people of Canada either.
In a country which boasted of the magnificent work accomplished, the work done through the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, a country which could find $10,000,000 a day to save ourselves in Europe, a country which can boast of that fact-perhaps I should not say "boast", but is certainly proud of it -can we find only $5,000,000 to rehabilitate
2.500	homes, many of which are under ten feet of water today, their entire life savings gone, not a particle of crop for one, two or three years, not a bit of feed for their cattle for at least a year or two? Do you tell me we can find only $5,000,000 today, and that out of that there must be deducted amounts paid to the army? I want to pay my compliments-

speechtext:
I am glad pay and allowances are not included, because I wish to tell the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman,

Supply-Finance
that I had the privilege of escorting the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and it was not on one of these conducted tours. I conducted him personally around where the houses were floating and where only small portions of telegraph poles were showing. There were enough brass hats around there to sink a ship, and if we had to pay them, God help us. I know what I am talking about. I did not take any conducted tour around there. I went around in a small boat, in row boats and "ducks". I know what I am talking about, irrespective of what anyone may say.
Maybe I am bitter; I know I am bitter. I saw there people I have known all my lifetime. My father sold them their farms forty years ago. They were the people who pioneered, and who by their hard work brought up their families-families who enlisted-did it voluntarily, and fought for their country. Many of them did not come back. They built that country. And now to see these pioneers lose their all, with not one word being mentioned by this government to date, except the responsibility they have to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, is not easy to take. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company did not assume its fair responsibilities. Not one acre of that land would be under water today if the president of the Canadian Pacific and his fellow directors had done the decent and the honest thing as Canadian citizens, and had not deliberately lied as they did in the letter referred to by the Minister of Transport.
Of course I am bitter. I would like the minister and some of his colleagues to look at some of these pictures. They would see barns floating down the river, out to the Pacific, I suppose, on their way to my good friend's own riding.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I was there.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
Oh, the minister may have been there; but I lived there all my life. I did not just tour over it. I went through it in a row boat, in a small boat, and I know what I am talking about. I do not want any corrections from him in that matter.
I know the government will do the right thing, at least I believe it will. I honestly believe it will, because I believe that the present Prime Minister and his successor, whoever he may be, are good men. They will be good Canadian citizens and want to do the right thing for their fellow Canadians, irrespective of party. I believe that no matter what party he belongs to, the leader of that party wrants to do the right thing for his fellow citizens.
But I do believe this, that no man has any justification for standing up in front of me and telling me that we can find $10,000,000 a day for destruction in wartime, and then
try to justify an estimate of only $5,000,000 for the rehabilitation of this area. I do not 'believe that is the wish of the Canadian people.
I do not believe it is the desire of the Canadian people or of the Canadian government. I do not believe it is their intention.
Unfortunately, however, there are statements by people who have not the human touch, who have not had first-hand information-
I will not go so far as to say they have not wanted to know-and who have not firsthand knowledge. They cannot tell me that this is a proper amount. I am appealing to the government and, through the government to parliament here in Ottawa, to say to the government that that is not sufficient for the rehabilitation of 2,500 of their fellow citizens, pioneers of this country who did not inherit silver spoons, who did not make their profits in wartime companies. All they have today- the homes they built, and everything they owned-was gained by the sweat of their brows and by their hard work. Surely they are entitled to every consideration.
I believe the people of Canada would endorse any move the government would make to rectify this situation.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
I do trust that the government will pay heed to the remarks just made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. As he has said, the Fraser valley has been his home throughout the whole of his lifetime. He knows the conditions there better than anyone in Ottawa, and he is thoroughly qualified to place the facts before the house. I, for one, would not think of questioning his statement. So I do hope that the government will pay heed to his representations.
One thing that worries me greatly about the proposed settlement is that it is a settlement for cash, before anyone knows the extent of the damage. The Prime Minister announced the other day that the dominion government would pay $5,000,000, and that that constituted the full settlement of its liability for rehabilitation and emergency relief.
As the hon. member for Fraser Valley has said, a good deal of the land is still under water. It is impossible to determine at this time what the total damage will be. I suggest, that the dominion should not make a final settlement now, but that there should be some provision for further assistance, if it is found that the cost of rehabilitation and of emergency relief exceeds $10,000,000. I presume the idea was that the dominion would pay half and the province half, I hope that the dominion will not insist on this $5,000,000
Supply-Finance

being a final settlement if it is found that the damage exceeds twice that figure.
There is a further payment to be made in connection with the repairing of dikes. We should have some assurance from the government that when they are built again they wrill be modern dikes, no matter what the cost. I do not know whether this estimate of $4,500,000 will provide for three-quarters of the cost of modem dikes.
