speechtext: Is it a term of the agreement that these dikes will be of the modern type mentioned by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, wide enough at the top to allow for a line of trucks in either direction? Can either of the ministers tell me whether or not that is the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: The dike authority which is to be set up will have to advise the respective governments as to what type of dike would be best. Broadly speaking, it should be a modem type, adequate to perform the functions which it is supposed to perform, and if possible to make sure that there will be no recurrence of the disaster which occurred this year. It would be throwing money away if that were not done.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: I am glad that is so.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: Can the hon. member tell me the assessed value of the farms that have been flooded?

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot do that. The hon. member for Fraser Valley has set the number at 2,500. I doubt if he would know the assessed value of those farms, because many municipalities are involved. The actual damage caused by the flood cannot be determined as yet, because the flood is still there. Much of the land is still under water, and that is why I cannot understand the dominion making a final settlement at this time. I think it was premature to set a final figure.
I should like to express a word of appreciation for the way in which the people of the other provinces came to the help of the sufferers in the Fraser valley area. Our province is a long way from eastern Canada; we face the Pacific rather than the Atlantic, and I 
suppose we sometimes feel that we have been forgotten and are not getting a fair deal. It is easy for us to develop antagonism toward the other parts of Canada. I cannot remember anything in my lifetime that has done more to drive away that feeling than the manner in which the cities and towns and villages in other parts of Canada voluntarily offered help to their fellow citizens in the Fraser valley.
Right from the start, almost before the government in Ottawa realized that this was a national emergency-I am not blaming anyone at the moment-funds were being donated in Montreal and Toronto to help the sufferers, under a lead given by the mayors of those two cities. Similar help has been received from other centres and organizations in eastern Canada and we are all most grateful. It makes us all just that much more proud to be Canadians. I am sure I speak for all the members from British Columbia when I express that word of appreciation to our fellow Canadians in the other eight provinces.
One other fine feature was the spirit shown by these people who had to get out of their homes, leave their furniture behind and, in some cases, lose their stock. They accepted all these hardships with remarkable spirit; very much the spirit that the hon. member for Fraser Valley has shown here, very much the spirit that he showed during the first world war when he had such a wonderful record. The people of his valley have certainly shown themselves to be a grand lot.
I was proud, too, of the help given by my city of Vancouver, by the city of New Westminster and 'by the adjoining areas. Businessmen, workers in factories and school boys all went out night after night to work on the dikes. They received no pay; it was entirely a voluntary effort and they did a grand1 job. Many United States citizens voluntarily crossed the line from' the neighbouring state of Washington to lend a hand, which was a very fine action. These kindly, helpful acts were the bright spots in this terrible catastrophe, the worst in the history of the province.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: This session should prorogue in glory after the fine speech of my fine friend.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
I should like to support everything said by the hon. member for Vancouver South and the tributes he has paid. I also support his remarks as to the undesirability of the dominion making a final settlement of $5,000,000 for relief and rehabilitation. It is estimated that the damage in the Fraser valley alone will amount to $30,000,000, and that does not take into account the damage in

Supply-Finance
other portions of the province. That being the case, I think it is premature for the federal government to say this represents a final settlement with respect to their contribution toward compensation for damages. I consider it desirable that they make a cash contribution now, .but I think they should leave the door open for the payment of an increased sum when the amount of actual damage is finally assessed.
I find it difficult to understand why the premier of the province accepted1 that small payment. We should approach this whole matter in a spirit of co-operation. The hon. member for Vancouver South has mentioned how much we appreciate the co-operation of citizens all over Canada, but I would point out that, according to the figures tabled during this session, it is shown that, under the financial agreement between the dominion and the province of British Columbia, the dominion takes in tax revenue from that province $144,000,000 and returns just over $20,000,000. This means that the tax resources of the provinces are extremely limited.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: That ridiculous argument always irritates me beyond question. Dominion taxes -would have been no lower in British Columbia if we were not paying British Columbia $20,000,000.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
What the minister has said has not disproved my argument, because those tax fields are now occupied exclusively by the federal government. This means that the tax resources of the province are that much more limited, that there is that much less in the way of free sources of revenue from which to meet the tremendous burden imposed by the flood disaster. As I say, it is estimated that the damage is $30,000,000, of which the province will evidently have to find $25,000,000, while the dominion finds only $5,000,000. I do not think one is extreme when he says that is ungenerous treatment. I am surprised that the premier of the province would have concluded this agreement and accepted this figure of $5,000,000 as a final payment.
There are one or two other matters which I think should be mentioned. While it is a source of satisfaction to find that money is being provided for the repairing of the dikes in the Fraser valley, it is a source of concern to find that as yet no effort is made to prevent floods at the source. I shall not go into that because we discussed it previously, but if we are to prevent floods in the future it is not enough merely to provide dikes in the Fraser river valley down in the broad flat lands, but care must be taken to prevent a rapid runoff at the head waters.
Finally I think we are entitled to expect to find some item for compensation of the provincial government for the expenses which it incurs in carrying out this program of rehabilitation and the assessment and repairing of damaged lands. The Minister of Fisheries has made it quite clear that the dominion government has handed over the responsibility for the administration to the province, and I think that is proper, because they are close to the spot; they know the needs and they can administer relief more efficiently. But obviously it will be an expensive thing to administer. The province will have to send their own officials and probably will have to employ more experts and so on. While it is proper to leave the detailed administration to the province, the expenses incurred in that administration should be taken into consideration in fixing the amount which the federal government will grant to the province over and above the $5,000,000 as straight compensation, which, as I have said, I do not consider adequate. While some if not most of the things I have said may have been critical, I, like other members, appreciate to the full the generous gestures made by private citizens, the work of the armed forces, and so on, but I do think the rest of the citizens of Canada and the federal government should have all the facts placed before them, so they they may be able to judge whether or not some further compensation should be paid to the province, and whether or not the door should be held open, instead of being closed on this question of the provision of a further cash payment when the amount of damages is finally assessed.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
I wish to add one word. Perhaps an Ontario man should not step into this, but one or two things can be suggested. First, this is a national emergency. That has been shown by the action of the government. Second, for the moment an agreement has been arrived at, in which the province of British Columbia, in the view of some British Columbia members seems to have made an improvident agreement. But when we talk about things being final, I do not think that in a democracy things are ever final, because public opinion can always assert itself and the public will want the right thing done in the end, once the damages are assessed. The damages may be more, or they may be less. But this is a step forward. The door is not banged and barred and bolted, and I suggest that we might take what has been done as so much gained.
Supply-Finance

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
I have listened with great respect to the remarks of the hon. member for Fraser Valley, who has made himself the voice of his countrymen in that area. While it is pardonable for the hon. member for Fraser Valley to be emotional, since he is deeply affected personally and since he is one of the people, I feel that we, the remaining members of the house and I myself as one coming from the province which is affected, should be strictly practical about what is to be done with the sum allotted by the government. I think we should make certain that what is done with it will result in something of permanent value to the people of the Fraser valley.
It is extremely difficult to assess in dollars and cents what the final results of the flood will be, but it is not difficult to assess the steps that can now be taken with regard to fhe diking and harnessing of the Fraser river. As I said in an earlier debate, the condition of the Fraser river is and has been changing for some fifty years. That river has reached geological maturity. Its course, if left unregulated, will change and will result in damage to the lands now cultivated on its banks. There is only one possible solution. That solution lies in the report of engineers who are capable of assessing the conditions in that area and of deciding what type of dikes shall be built and how much money should be spent. After that, while we cannot talk in terms of a Canadian T.V.A., nevertheless it will probably be found that if money is wisely spent in that area power from the Fraser can be harnessed, lands irrigated, and secondary industries will flourish at the mouth of the Fraser, and the people of the Fraser river valley will be properly protected. But that will require the employment of sums far in excess of the 810,000,000 proposed. I would ask the minister to take into consideration plans for the future, rather than to regard this as a temporary emergency.
Our geologists and our departments are aware that the flood of 1894 was as great as the flood which has just taken place. There are a great many years between 1894 and 1948; but, since none of us can say what nature will do in any particular year, the flood of this year could be repeated ten years later. It is obvious that it is entirely up to man, with the modern machinery and modern methods at his disposal, to harness these things and to make this valley safe and to turn the present disadvantages into advantages for industry.
I,	too, went over the flooded area in an aeroplane. My riding had the honour of

entertaining six cabinet ministers at one time who flew over that area, and it was an aweinspiring sight to see that valley from the air in its flooded condition. But knowledge of the actual situation cannot be gained in that way. The people who live in that area and the people of the province feel that they have been let down, because there has been no planning on the part of government which would have rendered the flood at least less damaging. If there had been large planning much might have been saved that was lost. I think there is a lesson to be found in the Fraser river valley flood if the government and the departments care to learn it, and that is that we must be practical, we must plan, and not just say:	We are going to spend $10,000,000,
and that relieves us of further responsibility. The government must not wash its hands of the situation once that $10,000,000 has been spent. I urge that the government and the minister make a definite statement that they accept responsibility with regard to the unassessed damages of this flood.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
I was one of the members representing one of the other districts that suffered during the disaster. Perhaps the committee will bear with me while I occupy a few minutes of its time. May I, first of all, join with the hon. member for Vancouver South in his remarks where he gave credit to the wonderful help and assistance rendered by all persons in all walks of life. It is amazing how the Canadian people rise to the occasion when called upon to do so. When the call went forth to men and women for help to man the canteens there was a ready response from one end of the country to the other. I want to take a minute to add my word of praise for the wronderfuI help and assistance given. Then, of course, there is the great fund of money which is being collected from all over. Other countries as well have contributed.
However I want to pass from that and say a word or two regarding the flood itself. Many statements have been made regarding what it will cost. I am one of those who believe that no one can estimate or tell just what the actual damage will be until the water is actually off the land. It is natural that the hon. member for Fraser Valley should be wondering whether the $5,000,000 allotted is sufficient to take care of rehabilitation. My own view is that it is not. On the other hand, I have a statement made by the government, and I do not think they will deny it, that they are willing to pay 75 per. cent of the cost of diking, and that they have also agreed with the province to pay for complete rehabilitation. While it is easy for some of us, including myself, to rise in our places and advocate this

Supply

Finance
or that, yet one cannot overlook the fact that the provincial government whose responsibility it is, and who have assumed the job of rehabilitation-I do not think there is any argument on that-did meet all the reeves of the affected areas, seven in number, including a number of councillors. They met at a place called Murrayville in the constituency of New Westminster. Assurance was given by the provincial minister of municipalities, the Hon. R. C. MacDonald, who is in charge. The following appeared in the British Columbian Weekly of June 21:
Mr. MacDonald told the gathering that the provincial government was prepared for the complete rehabilitation of the flood victims and he was in complete charge. He felt that administration of the assistance could be handled more efflciently through the local flood committees which have been established in each area.
In many oases the farmers themselves will be able to do much of the repair work on their homes and barns and for this the provincial government will pay them.
There you have a meeting of all concerned right on the ground. The hon. member for Fraser Valley may have information that I have not, but the reeves of my own district have not complained about the agreement already entered into by the provincial and dominion governments. They met on the job with the provincial minister there, who has given the assurance that full rehabilitation will be .taken care of under the guidance and jurisdiction of the provincial authorities.
With regard to the $4,500,000 for dikes, I doubt whether the provincial grant added to the $4,500,000 for dikes will mean that they will be able to spend more than that until March of next year.
May I say this to the committee. I believe that some good will ultimately come out of the flooded areas, because for the first time the attention of the dominion government has been drawn to the conditions on the Fraser river, and to the lands through which the Fraser river flows. It is true that we have been complaining about the lack of dikes, but diking out there is not a simple matter. I am going to draw to the attention of the committee just one little problem that will arise in regard to diking. Diking on the river is just one aspect of the diking of the Fraser valley. In my riding I have groups of farmers who have diked against the sea, and who are being charged up to $7.50 an acre, and will be for the next fifty years. They come to me and say, "If the dominion and the provincial governments are to build dikes to protect the lands from the waters of the Fraser they had better dike ours against the ravages of the sea." I mention that to show the committee 5849-388
just one of the many problems that will arise. I ask the hon. member for Vancouver South how he would settle that.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: You had better settle it yourself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
I have to give them an answer. I shall be inclined to support them in their view of making representations. That is just an example of what is apt to happen when we start to rehabilitate
I have every sympathy for the groups flooded out .and the residents who will have to be rehabilitated. It will be a stupendous task. It is a task that will require the services of men .with sympathy and a little firmness in deciding the cases that will come before them.
In my own district 4,000 acres were under water. It is true that a greater .part of the constituency of New Westminster is protected by diking. The dikes helped. Like the dikes in the Fraser Valley riding, these dikes were all built by the farmers themselves. They are apt to say, Now, we want some further protection from the government because if they are going to do 140 miles of diking on the Fraser river, build modern dikes so that you can drive two trucks across it, we had better have the same kind of protection for our land. I thought it my duty to mention that >to the committee.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley knows the conditions there perhaps better than anyone else. I do not know whether he has the double trouble of diking from the sea, but I know I have it in my own riding. I thought I should rise at this time, first of all to express my appreciation of the great help that has been given by thousands of volunteer workers. It is true there was a little dispute here and there between the military personnel and the civil population. That was only to be expected, because the civil population thought that many of the army men should take off their army boots and go down in gum-boots and overalls, wade through the water, and start packing sandbags. Apart from that, things were handled remarkably well.
What the dikes will cost, no one can say. What rehabilitation and relief will cost no one can estimate at the present time. Someone has said $30,000,000. My own belief is that, until the water has all subsided and conditions improve, it will be impossible to tell exactly what damage has been done. Some will be greatly damaged; many will be wiped out; others may well be slightly benefited, because much of the land received a coating of silt. Provided that the land does
Supply-Finance

not receive too heavy a coat of silt, it may do the land considerable good in places. I think the hon. member for Fraser Valley would agree with that statement. Those who had strawberries or raspberries and find them buried under the silt will find that they are gone, and they will not have another crop until they replant and wait for two or three years.
But these are all matters which will be gone into by the local committees. I am pleased indeed to note that the provincial government has set these committees in motion, has called all the reeves and councillors together and discussed with them right on the ground where the damage can be seen. They are in the best position to know exactly what should be done. Our position should be to pay them enough money and to leave it to the provincial and municipal authorities to carry out their task. I say that without fear of successful contradiction.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
Mr. 'Chairman, I think it is established' that what happened dn the Fraser valley is a national disaster, and that the hon. member for Fraser Valley, in whose district it took place, should feel strongly about it is not to be wondered at. In fact, it would be strange if he did not. But the position in which I find myself is this. In the agreement that has been made there has been not only the dominion government but the provincial government, and I understand that the provincial premier was here. I do not know whether he met or asked to see other members of parliament. Certainly he did not ask to see me. If he is satisfied with the arrangement made with the government it would be presumptuous of me to say that the agreement was not a good' one.
But what I am glad to find out tonight is that this amount is not a hard and fast one beyond which the government will not go. If I correctly understood the remarks of those who spoke before me, this is at least the amount that can be properly spent this year in rehabilitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext: No. That relates to the diking work; that is the $4,500,000.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
The other, the rehabilitation, as has been so well pointed out by other hon. members who have spoken, cannot in my opinion be ascertained until the water has receded and the proper investigations have been made and the damage estimated. That will be the proper time to set the figure. As has been pointed out, some people will be put out of production for perhaps a couple of years. Others may not be affected very much.
Perhaps the people in other parts of Canada do not appreciate how important the IVaser

valley is to British Columbia. It is important if for no other reason than the fact that it supplies nearly all the fluid milk for a population of over 300,000 in greater Vancouver.
As I said before, I am in a difficult position because I cannot start to criticize the British Columbia government for not safeguarding the interests of the people of the district, since I do not know all the facts.

maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few more words to say, and I admit frankly that possibly I am, not unnecessarily, but excessively bitter. I represent at least ninety-five per cent of the people in the flooded area. During the time the flood was at its height, on one occasion I got in contact with my home by telephone, and my sister informed me that there was an urgent long distance call for me in Vancouver. When the second call came I took it, and the object of the call was for me to attend a by-election meeting in Vancouver. This was at seven o'clock at night. The one reason my telephone has not been taken out is that I have not lost the support of the hon. member for Mackenzie for the language I used.
Five minutes before, I heard a call for
1,000	volunteers for a certain area which I will not name, and then I am asked to leave when I am doing my duty, where the dike is threatened, in order to attend a political by-election. I was not there. If my language could have been heard there it would have flooded any dike.
I was the first one who said-I made the statement before I left Ottawa to return to the district-that no one could estimate the damage. I cannot on my own farm, nor can any member in the Fraser valley, estimate the damage to farm property that is anywhere from four feet to fifteen feet under water. Every newspaper in British Columbia, every radio station called me, and newspapers since I came back to Ottawa got in contact with me asking for my opinion on the damage. Government officials have asked me the same thing, and I replied that no one could estimate the extent of the damage caused by the flood.
As to the question of full rehabilitation, I wish to quote from a certain editorial and then I am through. I believe this editorial will substantiate what other members have said. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that this government is sincere in its desire to help, and so is parliament. I know the people of Canada are sincere in wishing to give all the assistance they can. I do not believe that the government, the department or the people of

Supply-Finance
Canada at this stage can estimate the extent of what is required to take care of the damage.
I am firmly of the opinion, howeyer, that what is needed is something considerable. If I suggested a blank cheque I would be going too far, perhaps, but almost a blank cheque such as we had in wartime is necessary. This parliament and the people of Canada should in my opinion give this government the necessary means to re-establish their fellow citizens in the Fraser valley or in any other part of Canada to meet a national disaster such as this.
I should like to quote a front-page editorial from the largest weekly newspaper in the affected district, the Chilliwack Progress. This editorial will give hon. members of this committee a good idea of the situation. I quote: They're Moving Back
Henry Jensen is tall, blonde, well built and Danish. He likes to wear a red baseball cap. He happens to be .a progressive farmer and an aggressive, independent and energetic citizen.
He was forced from his Arnold road farm by the flood waters from the Cannor breakthrough. Friday, Henry Jensen and his friends got his cattle together; piled his possessions on a truck and set off down the Liekman road to home.
The Jensens were luckier than a good many people. He lost 'his crops but the flood didn't reach the main floor of his home. He's not discouraged and neither is his Vancouver bred wife.
For the last two weeks, he's been hearing government warnings, regulations, vague promises and announcements of plans to help him and others like him. He was anxious, like hundreds of others, to get back. He was one of the few who could go back. He couldn't afford to wait while governments bridged the time gap between when they said they were going to do something and when they actually do it.
Everyone knows machinery fop relief and rehabilitation can't be set .up overnight, but there has been an unnecessary amount of backing and filling by departments concerned; a reluctance to assume immediate responsibility and to back up announced plans with action.
The Shortage of hay, even for temporary feeding of livestock, is for instance, critical. Immediate supplies are needed. People are still vague about who they are to see about health regulations; others are wandering around trying to find someone who is responsible for assessing damages to homes and barns. People have been moving back for .a week now'. It is later than the government thinks. The Jensens, the Toopa have returned.
In none of the government's actions, however, is there evidence of insincerity-
I want the minister to note this.
-or a backing down on its promises. The problem is one of putting words into action.
To make political capital of the flood and its aftermath, as was done in '94, is abhorrent. It is nonsense to say the government is responsible for the flood. They must, however, with all of us, help clean up the aftermath and take steps 6849-388J
to see that every possible means is employed to prevent a repetition of breaks in the diking system. They must see-with us-that a fair and equitable system of assessment of damages and payment of claims is worked out.
It is a big job and we should get on with it.
Is there anything unreasonable in that frontpage editorial appearing in the largest weekly newspaper in the affected district? The only thing I wish to say in that connection was brought out during my absence at the request of the Canadian Legion of the Fraser valley, and that is the excessive cost of hay. Today hay is $36 a ton.
Chilliwack and the Fraser valley ask for consideration by the government and by parliament, not on party lines but as aid to our fellow Canadians.

speechtext:
I wish to move an amendment to item 83. I move:
That item 83 be reduced to one dollar.
I do this with a full realization that it hits at the major problem and one of the major planks of the government's policy of economic control. I feel that at the present time the foreign exchange control board and the artificial restrictions imposed on our trade with the United States are among the major contributory causes to the inflationary pressure which is being built up on the Canadian price structure. To illustrate my contention, I should like to quote from the current issue of the Canadian Statistical Review, just published for the month of May by the dominion bureau of statistics. Discussing the importance or the lessening of our unfavourable balance of trade with the United States, they say this:
Our unfavourable balance of trade with the United States for this period has fallen from $295 million in 1947 to about $156 million in the current year. But this improved trade position has meant that fewer imported goods have been available for the domestic market, while more of our own production has been going abroad. Although our imports from all countries are up by $27 million or by about three per cent, when allowance is made for the rise in prices, the actual volume has probably fallen.
Then it goes on:
With incomes earned in Canada continuing to rise-total labour income for the first quarter of the year was up $194 million over the same period a year ago-the demand for all types of consumer goods has remained high and this has almost inevitably resulted in a further upward pressure on price levels. The one important limiting factor has been the substantial surplus of the Canadian government.
I mentioned that before. Then it goes on to say:
As long as individuals, business firms, governments and foreign buyers try to spend funds in excess of current income the pressure toward higher price levels will continue.
There is one other sentence I should like to read, and I am endeavouring not to remove these extracts from their context. This last sentence is as follows:
As consumer goods accumulate and individuals' most urgent needs are filled, they become more willing to increase their rate of saving. Similarly as new plants are built business requirements for capital become less acute and this decline in the demands for new equipment also helps remove the upward pressure on prices.
I contend that the imposition of exchange restrictions is having the direct effect of pushing up prices, and that, by so restricting our trade with the United States, it is not only causing a certain amount of ill feeling but, further than that, preventing that necessary flow of free trade between our two countries.
I feel that at the present time we are losing a tremendous volume of United States funds which would come to Canada for capital investment, come to Canada for the sake of building new plants.
I realize that great strides have been made in the construction of new plants. I feel that we may feel satisfied, in our own Canadian way; ibut we, on this North American continent, are lagging behind the increased productivity and increased industrial expansion of the country to the south of us. I consider that that is definitely, at least partly, caused by the restrictions on our exchange of currency.
We are in a singularly fortunate position.
I believe that our economy, our natural resources, and the development of our potential natural wealth makes our economy free enough and strong enough to withstand the impact of a free exchange. I believe that we have undeveloped in Canada the greatest natural potential, particularly in things of which the United States is short, including base metals, as well as other products. At the present time I am speaking of non-farm products. I believe our economy can complement the United States economy, and that there are literally billions of dollars waiting for investment in Canada from the United States.
I say, further, that the impact of this money upon the development and investment market in Canada would have a tendency to keep our two exchanges in a state of comparative equilibrium. I do not think there is a danger of the Canadian dollar selling at a great discount. I believe that the advantage to the economy of Canada in having a truly international dollar, exchangeable into United States dollars, and exchangeable freely without let or hindrance, anywhere in the world, would be such an advantage to the Canadian economy that it must be seriously considered at the present time.
I realize that the Foreign Exchange Control Act ends on March 31, 1949. I believe that we are in a potentially strong enough position to free our dollar from controls now. I feel that the goods which we have and which the world must have, to exist, would guarantee that the Canadian dollar would become one of the most sought after currencies of the whole world. Furthermore, the freedom of capital to come into and leave Canada without restriction, let or hindrance would, in my opinion, bring in such an influx of develop-
Supply-Finance

ment capital that it would greatly solve our present adverse 'balance of trade with the United States.
For these reasons I have offered my amendment.

The stenographers on the House of Commons staff are employed between sessions in other departments of government. Up to a year ago they were given the grade II maximum, and received $143 a month. I understand that a year ago, on instructions of the Department of Finance, they received the grade II minimum, or $120 a month with reductions, which gave them a cheque of $103.
This is a drastic reduction, and these girls find it hard to make ends meet. I might say that, through this reduction, they are being trimmed of about $45 a month. There is the $23 reduction from the higher to the lower grade, and $22 as an allowance for the 28 per cent increase in living costs.
We cannot expect to have expert stenographers on the House of Commons stenographic staff if that is the way in which they are to be treated. It is no encouragement for them.
I must say that the permanent civil service is receiving increases and has permanent employment. Apparently this is the only group being discriminated against. speechtext:
I should like to have a few more words with the minister about the wartime prices ian-d tra-de board and this question- of the re-imposition of price controls and subsidies. I hope -that we are now able to discuss this matter in a little more reasonable atmosphere than was the case for a number of months prior to last night. Until last night any request from this corner of the house for a reimposition of -price controls and subsidies was met with a negative reply. The minister has told -us on occasion that it could be done only by the restoration of wage controls. He has told ,us on other occasions that some controls were being maintained in so far as that

Supply-Finance
was permitted by the parliamentary statute, but it was clear that the general approach of the government was negative.
However, we now have the adoption of the prices committee report, which, although it did not go down the line for over-all price controls, suggested that some controls and subsidies should be put back on. Earlier this evening I felt that the minister indicated a slight change of attitude, in that he stated that the recommendations of the committee as approved by the house would be given immediate consideration. I should like the minister to recall a question which was asked him last Thursday by my colleague, the hon. member for Churchill, and which had to do with the minister's promise earlier this year that if prices of meat and butter got out of hand controls would be reimposed. That promise took the form of a statement which the minister made on March 4 of this year, as reported on pages 1864 and 1865 of Hansard in reply to a question by the hon. member for Lethbridge. On that occasion the hon. member asked this same question. I think I Should give the committee the text of the minister's answer on that date. This is the Minister of Finance speaking:
Perhaps I had better answer that question. The situation with respect to ceilings on meat, including beef, is this. The government announced late in January, I think, that it intended to reimpose ceilings on meat and on butter; and it was pointed out at that time that the imposition of retail ceilings on meat involved quite a technical operation in working out what those ceilings should be with respect to, I am told, nearly 200 items. That work has been proceeded with _ and it is now completed; but in the meantime tire retail prices of meats are somewhat below the prices which were prevailing at the time the announcement was made, and therefore there has been no necessity to impose the formal ceilings. As I say, the technical work has been done, and in the event of its being necessary to do so, ceilings can be reimposed promptly.
As long ago as March 4 the minister indicated that the technical work, even though it was complicated and involved nearly 200 meat items, had been completed and that the government was in a position, through the medium of the wartime prices and trade board, to put ceilings back on if the same became necessary. I should like to ask the minister what work has been done in the meantime by the wartime prices and trade board to get ready to put ceilings back on as might now be desirable in view of the approval that this house gave to the report of the prices committee. It seems to me that the argument which the government has used in the past Should not now be used because of the action taken last night by this house and
because of the at least slight change in attitude shown by the minister earlier this evening when he said that immediate consideration would be given to this report.
I know something of the splendid work the wartime prices and trade board did in the years when the government gave it half a chance, and it would seem to me that that board would now have some machinery ready and some of the technical work done, so that it would be possible for the government to act upon the report of the prices committee.
I am not now asking the minister for a restatement of the promise he made at eight o'clock; I am asking him to state what plans have been worked out and what work has been done by the wartime prices and trade board to get ready to carry out an anticipated change in government policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERATED CO-OPERATIVES OF SASKATCHEWAN- SUPPLY OF STEEL RODS

If it were decided to reimpose ceilings, on meat for instance-I am not prepared to say that would be a desirable thing- it would be necessary for the prices board to do a considerable amount of technical work; it would be necessary to call in the trade and make quite an extensive study. Retail ceilings on meat is a complicated matter. Meat prices have already moved through the ceilings to which I referred last January. This sort of thing works both ways and the producers may have some interest in the matter.
To answer my hon. friend's question directly, it would be necessary for the prices board to do a considerable amount of work in order to be ready to reimpose ceilings on meat. So far that work has not been done.
